After Trump was elected president of the United States, the global economy faced greater uncertainty. After the new US government took office, the direction of US policy may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—which may have profound implications for the global economy landscape. It is worth noting that the pace of interest rate hikes in the US, the strengthening of the US dollar, and the possibility of the US adopting trade protectionist measures have exacerbated the risks faced by emerging market economies. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained relatively stable, while Hong Kong bank interbank lending rates have risen along with US dollar interbank lending rates. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remain good, and overall loan growth further increased in the second half of 2016. Following the implementation of the new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. Looking ahead, banks should cautiously assess the possibility that the pace of US interest rate hikes may be faster than expected, as well as the impact of uncertainty in US policy on a broader level, particularly the risk of large-scale capital outflows and the potential effect on Hong Kong interest rates. After Trump was elected president of the United States, the global economy faced greater uncertainty. Not only did the election results surprise the market, but the related market reaction was also unexpected. In particular, expectations that measures such as the tax reform introduced by Trump, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation will drive US economic growth are propelling the global stock market upward. After the new government took office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects—from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalization to anti-globalization—or will have profound implications for the global economy landscape. However, the market's expectation that Trump's tax cuts will not generate the anticipated stimulus to US economic growth. Especially as current US economic activity is approaching its potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only bring a mild cyclical stimulus effect to US economic growth, but will exacerbate the risk of rising US inflation. Although it remains unknown whether the US Federal Reserve will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening because of this, long-term bond yields have clearly risen, partially reflecting market expectations that inflation risk is increasing. At the same time, the rise of trade protectionist measures will cause a "double loss" for the US and other regions worldwide. Increased trade barriers will distort the market, harm overall interests, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and bring downside risks to the global economy outlook. At the same time, unstable political situations remain a major risk and unfavorable factor, especially for the European economy, which is still weak in its recovery. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflow has increased due to the accelerating pace of US interest rate hikes and the further appreciation of the US dollar. This may drag down economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflow. In fact, anticipating that the Trump administration will implement large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns over surging energy prices, the market has repriced for inflation risk, leading to a comprehensive and significant rise in long-term bond yields across developed economies and several emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hikes on the sovereign bond market of 26 selected economies. Research results indicate that since the "reduce buying panic" in 2013, the impact of the US Treasury bond market on the sovereign bond market has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tighter financial conditions will have a significant impact on developed economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, with the rebound in exports, economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, but market fluctuations such as currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields in the region, which were previously caused by concerns over potential policy changes by the new US government, gradually stabilized by the beginning of this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain stable growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces are also increasing. US interest rate hikes, currency depreciation in the region, and increased volatility in the financial market may lead to tighter financial conditions. At the same time, the US may implement protectionist policies, which may affect the regional economy, but the actual impact is not yet clear. In mainland China, the overall economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, driven by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilization, the growth prospects in China remain uncertain. Especially in the situation where the government is determined to curb housing price increases, if the real estate market continues to cool down, the contribution of the real estate industry to growth this year may decrease. At the same time, the continued promotion of economic structure adjustment and the changes in China-US trade relations may increase the uncertainty of the short-term economy outlook. Externally, although the RMB maintained stability against a basket of currencies at the China Foreign Exchange Trade Center (CFETS) during the reporting period, capital outflow pressure increased at the end of 2016 due to the appreciation of the US dollar and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently seemed to slightly ease in early 2017. Although the private sector's economic activity shows signs of recovery, there are still some concerns in the market regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy, especially given that M1 growth is accelerating while M2 growth is slowing down in the economy. Special Topic 2 (see page 24) explores the question of whether the China economy is trapped in a liquidity trap, and Special Topic 3 (see page 27) investigates the factors that may lead to a divergence between M1 and M2 growth. Research results indicate there is no evidence that China has fallen into a liquidity trap, and the main reasons why M1 growth has significantly outpaced M2 are the reduced opportunity cost of holding liquid currency due to recent monetary easing, and the increased economic uncertainty which may have increased precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong economy growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016. Quarterly real local GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Locally, private consumption continues to strengthen, and infrastructure activities booming in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, the growth in goods exports has risen with the improvement in intra-regional trade flows, while service exports are growing steadily with the recovery of trade-related and transportation services. Due to the faster growth in imports of goods and services, net exports will continue to drag down the growth of real local GDP in the second half of the year. With the rise in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate slightly decreased to 3.3% in December of the economy. The economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The government and market consensus forecasts for the growth of real local GDP in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0%, respectively. However, the growth prospects of Hong Kong still face significant external obstacles. The protectionist tone of the new US government increases the downside risks faced by global trade and external demand in Hong Kong. Facing pressure from the appreciation of the US dollar and the expectation of accelerated US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to reduce support for the real economy, and in the event of tail risks emerging, this may lead to tighter financial conditions Locally. Special Topic 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of the Hong Kong financial conditions index to assist in the supervision of financial conditions Locally. Since the second half of 2016, locally inflation pressure has remained mild, while the quarterly inflation momentum slightly accelerated in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to fluctuations in food prices and rising housing rents. Due to stable import prices, locally cost pressure is mild, and inflationary pressure is still controllable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained relatively stable, but it weakened somewhat after the US interest rate hikes in December. The redemption guarantee has not been triggered. With the appreciation of the US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar further rises. Due to the large monetary base, interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks remain low, but they have risen since October due to year-end funding demands and the recovery of US dollar interest rate hikes. Therefore, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October due to intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage interest rate slightly increased to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of the year, while growth in the first half of the year was 2.2%. Growth is supported by the strengthening of locally economic activity and the increased financing needs of multinational corporations in the economy at year-end. Locally loan growth accelerated slightly, while the use of loans outside Hong Kong decreased slightly in the first half of the year and then recovered. According to currency analysis, Hong Kong dollar loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans recorded a 3.2% increase as borrowers in China gradually reduced repayments of foreign currency loans. The bank's financial condition remains generally stable. The Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio slightly fell to 77.1%, the same as the end of 2016, reflecting that deposit growth exceeded loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% by year-end, and the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio significantly decreased to 63.8% due to strong US dollar deposit growth. Due to the strength of the US dollar, both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates have weakened. In this context, the offshore RMB fund pool in Hong Kong (including customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances) is further consolidating with other offshore RMB markets, and the volatility of offshore RMB interbank lending rates from Hong Kong banks has significantly increased. Nevertheless, the bank's management of RMB liquidity remains stable, and the average daily transaction amount in the RMB real-time payment settlement system remains at a high level. The offshore RMB business in Hong Kong will likely continue to face resistance from the uncertainty in the RMB exchange rate trend. With the improvement in global market conditions, the Hong Kong stock market experienced significant gains during the reporting period. Although the election of the president of the United States yielded unexpected results, the market only experienced a brief shock. This is mainly due to investors' anticipation of the Trump administration's fiscal stimulus measures, which drove the rise in global stock markets. Although benefiting from this, the Hong Kong market also showed prudence alongside optimism, the reasons possibly being concerns about the acceleration of US interest rate hikes, challenges facing the China economy, unclear RMB policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the Hong Kong market may be affected by external economic conditions, its valuation attractiveness can provide support to the market. Although the Hong Kong dollar bond yield rapidly increased at the end of last year, and the spread with US Treasury bonds rapidly widened, the Hong Kong dollar bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, the offshore RMB bond market in Hong Kong recovered in the second half of the year after contracting in the first half of the year, but the total issuance of new bonds for the full year was still less than the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their investment strategies that previously sought returns, both the Hong Kong dollar and the offshore RMB bond market will face pressure. Due to the lack of clarity in US trade policy, the RMB exchange rate may still fluctuate, and the outlook for both bond markets will continue to be troubled by significant uncertainties over the next six months. Following the government's introduction of new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. Given the renewed exuberance in the market, the government will raise the stamp duty to 15% in November. Trading volume in the primary and secondary market has declined in the last two months. However, trading volume has increased recently, partly reflecting the developer's increased launch of first-hand properties. Meanwhile, property prices continue to reach new highs, but the upward momentum is slowing down.

After Trump's unexpected victory as president of the United States, the uncertainty of U.S. policy increased. Although the market focus is on the short-term benefits brought by potential large-scale fiscal policies and business facilitation measures, the current US economic activity is nearing its potential, and fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical stimulus to US economic growth, but will further exacerbate the risk of inflation rising. More importantly, the risks faced by emerging market economies are increasing due to the pressure of capital outflows brought about by the acceleration of US interest rate hikes and the strengthening of the dollar, and potential trade protectionist measures by the United States will also threaten global trade. In East Asia, real economic activity slightly improved in the second half of 2016, and export volume has also increased recently. However, against the backdrop of interest rate hikes in the US, the appreciation of the dollar, and potential protectionist measures by the US, the financial market is expected to continue to fluctuate, and the downside risk to economic growth is increasing. In mainland China, the overall economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016, driven by robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector business expenditure. The domestic economy continues to rebalance, and the tertiary industry is steadily expanding, but the ongoing structural adjustments of the economy and the changes in China-US trade relations may increase short-term economic uncertainty. In the situation where the government is determined to curb housing price increases, if the real estate market continues to cool down, the contribution of the real estate industry to economic growth this year may also decrease. Externally, although the RMB maintained stability against a basket of currencies at the China Foreign Exchange Trade Center (CFETS) during the reporting period, capital outflow pressure increased at the end of 2016 due to the appreciation of the dollar and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently seemed to slightly ease in early 2017. After Trump's unexpected victory as president of the United States, the global financial market reacted strongly, especially as the market anticipated that Trump's implementation of tax reforms, large-scale infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth and inflation, stimulating the rise in major stock markets (Figure 2.1). Therefore, expectations for US inflation and US interest rate hikes in the market have risen, causing US Treasury bond yields to surge and the dollar to strengthen. (Figure 2.1) Stock indices of some advanced economies; however, the market expects that Trump's tax cuts may not have the positive impact on US economic growth that is expected by the market. Although economic policy shifting to rely on fiscal easing measures will help alleviate the heavy burden of monetary easing policies, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, the appropriateness of implementing fiscal easing measures at this time is debatable. Although the growth rate of the US economic activity has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the unemployment rate in February also met the Federal Reserve's estimate of the 4.7% natural rate of unemployment, reflecting that US economic activity is approaching its potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier will be lower than during a recession (for example, please refer to Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012) 1). In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve indicate that tax cuts in labor or capital may lead to a decrease in tax revenue (e.g., see Trabandt and Uhlig (2012)) 2. Regardless, in a situation of reduced excess capacity, any further measures to promote economic growth, even if the substantive impact on economic growth is limited, may increase inflation. Furthermore, rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures, including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, may exacerbate the upside risk of US inflation. Even though the risk of rising US inflation increases, the Federal Reserve remains cautious in tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partially reflecting increased US inflation risk. Since the US election, although the market's forecasts for future Federal Funds rate have been raised to near the median of the Federal Reserve's forecast for early 2017 and 2018, they remain significantly below the Federal Reserve's long-term forecast (Figure 2.2). Therefore, the acceleration of US interest rate hikes may trigger the risk of significant market volatility. Although the focus of the financial market is concentrated on the short-term benefits brought about by potential expansionary fiscal policies and business facilitation measures driving stronger economic growth in the US, long-term risks still exist, including detrimental protectionist trade policies and further increases in US national debt. In fact, the Trump government may fulfill its election promises by taking trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers will lead to market distortion, harm overall interests, impede global trade, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and bring downside risks to the global economic outlook. Figure 2.2 Future Federal Funds rate forecast: Political instability remains the main risk and obstacle to European economic recovery for the Federal Reserve and the market in Europe. Although the economic environment in the Eurozone is gradually improving, real Gross Domestic Product in the fourth quarter grew by 1.7% year-on-year, slightly lower than the 1.8% growth in the third quarter; however, compared to the stronger recovery of the US economic, economic activity in the Eurozone remains only slightly above pre-financial crisis levels (Figure 2.3). Since the decision to leave the UK last summer, the market has been concerned that the Eurozone will ultimately disintegrate. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilized after forming a new government and implementing measures to save the banking sector, the elections or meetings that Germany and France (possibly including Italy) are about to hold, against the backdrop of the UK Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, may become political flashpoints. Due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign bond yields in Europe continue to climb, and corporate bond spreads are also widening. This situation is particularly evident in neighboring countries and could create a vicious cycle for the real economy, potentially putting pressure on commercial real investment in the Eurozone. Figure 2.3 shows the real Gross Domestic Product of major advanced economies. For Japan, the real Gross Domestic Product has improved over the last few quarters, with the year-on-year growth rate for the fourth quarter of 2016 reaching 1.6%, the fastest growth since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger economic recovery than previously anticipated. However, some due to structural problems in the labor market have caused slow wage growth, leading to weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the Japanese yen has recently depreciated rapidly, meaning the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier appreciation of the yen is about to begin to ease. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery momentum, this indicates an improvement in the short-term inflation outlook, and although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and recover. Nevertheless, facing long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain slow, and inflation expectations are also maintained at approximately 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the level when the Bank of Japan launched its monetary easing in early 2014, thus the risk remains that the inflation rate will fail to reach the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2%. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits of faster economic growth through trade channels resulting from the US's reduced imports after the financial crisis and the possibility of the US implementing protectionist policies may be smaller. Meanwhile, the acceleration of US interest rate hikes and the further appreciation of the dollar will lead to tighter financial conditions and exacerbate economic downside risks. This may drag down economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflow. In fact, market expectations that the Trump government will implement large-scale fiscal expansion, coupled with concerns over surging energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risk, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across advanced economies and even some emerging market economies. Special Topic 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hikes on the sovereign bond market of 26 selected economies. In East Asia, real economic activity has recently recovered vitality, the local gross domestic product in the region has grown slightly, and inflation has risen. Real local gross domestic product growth — In the second half of 2016, due to stable private consumption in multiple regional economies, economic growth generally remained stable. Meanwhile, exports generally rose slightly from the low levels of 2015. This benefits not only from the stabilization of China's growth but also from the improved performance of advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (such as Malaysia and Indonesia), a rise in commodity prices also has an additional driving effect. Other major exporting countries (such as South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) are also regaining momentum due to the growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — With the rise in commodity prices (especially oil), producer price inflation is generally on the rise. Although this will increase industrial costs or consumption expenditures, consumption and investment growth may increase due to a decrease in the risk of long-term deflation. Accelerated producer price inflation or will exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which the increase in producer prices is passed on to consumption prices, and this is not uniform across different economies. Consensus forecasts for the consumption price index indicate that inflation in several economies within the region will still be slightly below the 2017 inflation targets of each central bank, but will rise to a level closer to the target (Figure 2.4). Excluding Indonesia, the central banks in the East Asia region generally maintained their accommodative monetary policies, while Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October of last year to stimulate growth. Figure 2.4 shows the inflation, forecast, and central bank target for the overall consumption price index in the East Asia region; although the real economy has improved, the result of the president of the United States election in November 2016 was unexpected, causing short-term volatility in the financial market. Foreign exchange market — after the president of the United States election, investors anticipate an increase in US inflation, and most currencies in the region will depreciate against the dollar. However, by trade-weighted measure, some currencies in the region depreciated less after the US election, or even slightly appreciated (Figure 2.5). Figure 2.5 Changes in Bond Market and Stock Market of Spot Foreign Exchange Depreciation Against the Dollar and Nominal Effective Exchange Rate After the US election — Asset prices temporarily declined after the president of the United States election but subsequently stabilized. The yield spread between sovereign bonds of economies in the East Asia region and US Treasury bonds is rising. However, as the market stabilized, the yields of some regional economies declined, but have not yet recovered to pre-election levels. (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, the interest rate differential has narrowed compared to before the election. (Figure 2.6) Investment flows of sovereign bonds and US Treasury bonds interest rate differential — Securities investment funds flowed out of the East Asia region in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "reduce buying panic" period in mid-2013. In the initial weeks of 2017, there was another inflow of funds, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth within the region is expected to remain stable, but the pace is still lower than the historical average. Due to the increasing uncertainty in US government policy and the uncertainty regarding the policy response from the Federal Reserve, the financial market is likely to remain volatile. The dollar and yield have risen significantly, which may attract funds to flow from within the region to the US, causing investors to reduce their investment in assets within the region, which is particularly worrying for assets whose current valuations are already high. Tightening of financial conditions in this situation will also cause enterprises with substantial debt denominated in dollar to face repayment pressure. Macroeconomically, the universal interest rate hikes globally will also lead to a decrease in fixed capital investment within the region, which not only burdens aggregate demand in the short term but may also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, exporting countries within the region face the potential threat of new trade protectionist measures being implemented by the US government's protectionist policies. The trade deficit between the US and East Asia economies has continued to expand in recent years (Figure 2.7), particularly in major export industries within the region, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. In the past twenty years, the US has seen an increase in imports in these industries and a large loss of employment positions. Those protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing may pose a significant risk to exporting countries within the region.

Private consumption growth accelerated and public sector building and construction activity boomed, driving a slight acceleration in Hong Kong's economic growth in the second half of 2016. Due to the increasing uncertainty in the external environment, the economic growth for 2017 is expected to be moderate. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflationary pressure is expected to remain under control. Hong Kong's economic growth slightly accelerated in the second half of 2016. Real Gross Domestic Product, adjusted for seasonal factors, grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Figure 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and a stable labor market situation, the rate of private consumption growth has accelerated, becoming the main driver of local gross domestic product growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong International Airport, building and construction activity has also become prosperous. However, due to weak corporate capital expenditure, the contribution of overall investment expenditure to local gross domestic product growth has narrowed. Externally, import and export of goods are accelerating in growth in line with the rise in intra-regional trade flows (Figure 3.2). Trade-related and transportation services are driving further growth in service exports, while service imports are rebounding partly due to strong tourism demand from local residents. Net exports continue to drag down the growth of the local gross domestic product. Figure 3.1 of the Real Gross Domestic Product growth rate and the contribution of major expenditure components, Figure 3.2. The real import and export labor market remains tight. The unemployment rate, adjusted for seasonal factors, remained at 3.4% in the first three quarters, and subsequently decreased slightly to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Figure 3.3). In fact, unemployment rates in several major industries have all decreased in the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation, and food service sectors, partly due to the stabilization of the retail sector's slowdown. The total number of employed persons reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labor force participation rate remained stable at approximately 61%. (Figure 3.3) The unemployment rate and the total number of employed persons are expected to keep real economic growth moderate in 2017. Regarding external factors, due to the uncertainty in the global macroeconomic and financial environment, global economic and trade growth is likely to remain moderate. In addition, the strength of the US dollar has led to an increase in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, which will suppress Hong Kong's export performance. Regarding local factors, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, the drag from rising interest rates suggests that private consumption is expected to grow modestly. With the increase in housing supply and the planned development of multiple infrastructure projects, building and construction activity is expected to grow steadily, but a sluggish business climate and rising interest rates will suppress corporate capital expenditure. The government currently forecasts that the Real Gross Domestic Product for 2017 will grow between 2% and 3%, while the average forecast by private sector analysts is 2.0% for the local gross domestic product. The prospects for economic growth are constrained by numerous uncertain factors, with the influence from the external environment being particularly significant. The policy uncertainty of the new United States government will make the global economic outlook unclear, and potential trade protectionist policies may bring obstacles to global trade flows. The process of the UK's withdrawal from the EU and elections in several major European countries may also lead to volatility in asset markets and affect the flow of funds in the Hong Kong dollar. Furthermore, the normalization of U.S. interest rates will tighten local currency conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has shown quarterly growth in recent months, the overall trend remains mild. Year-on-year comparison, the Consumer Price Index remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January of this year (Figure 3.4). The core inflation rate, reflecting the inflationary momentum calculated on a three-month to annual basis, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, subsequently slightly decreased to 2.4% in January. The main reasons for the rise in inflation are the increase in prices of traded goods and housing rents (Figure 3.5). In particular, the inflation of the prices of traded goods rose to 3.0% in the fourth quarter from the negative figure in the third quarter, mainly driven by the prices of basic food and clothing. At the same time, since the third quarter, with the narrowing decline in private housing rents and the increase in public housing rents in September 2016, the housing rents component of the Consumer Price Index rose, but subsequently slowed slightly in January (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 reflects different indicators of consumer price inflation, Figure 3.5 shows consumer price inflation classified by major components, and Figure 3.6 shows the Consumer Price Index for rent items and market rent. In the short term, due to weak import prices, local cost pressure is moderate, and expected inflationary pressure will remain under control. Due to the strength of the Hong Kong dollar in a certain extent offsetting the impact of the global commodity price rebound, import inflation will remain low (Figure 3.7). In the local area, the output gap for the fourth quarter is estimated to remain close to zero in 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressure and thus curb inflation in service-based items. Despite the tight labor market, wage increases have been modest in recent quarters, with per capita real wages rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 and subsequently falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Figure 3.8). Given the continued uncertainty in the external environment, leading to cautious business sentiment, the increase in labor costs should be restrained in this context. Furthermore, due to the poor retail sales performance over the recent months, the expected increase in retail property rents will be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the softening of private housing rents earlier will gradually emerge, and will also help alleviate inflationary pressure. Overall, it is expected that the annual inflation rate will decrease in 2017, and the government forecasts the core inflation rate for the full year to be 2.0%, which is low compared to 2.3% in 2016. Figure 3.7 commodity and import prices, Figure 3.8 unit labor costs and per capita real wages face upward and downward risks. Regarding downside risks, if the U.S. experiences accelerated inflation under a Trump government administration, it could lead to the U.S. raising interest rates faster than anticipated, or push up local mortgage interest rates, increasing downward pressure on property prices and housing rents. At the same time, an appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar will likely cause import prices to continue to weaken, and simultaneously diminish the local appeal to visitors to Hong Kong. Regarding upside risks, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it will accelerate the growth of Hong Kong's economic and push up international commodity prices driven by demand, thereby exerting upward pressure on local inflation. Furthermore, the increased statutory minimum wage will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may lead to further inflation, but the real impact of the inflation driven by this cost will depend on the extent to which labor costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite fluctuations in the financial markets, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained relatively stable, while Hong Kong bank interbank lending rates have risen along with US dollar interbank lending rates. Partly due to the improvement in the local economic environment, overall lending continues to grow moderately. Looking ahead, with the pace of US interest rate normalization accelerating, the direction of policy for the new US government being unclear, and political risks in Europe, volatility in Hong Kong dollar capital flows may increase. Despite fluctuations in the financial markets, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar has remained relatively stable (Figure 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November caused Asian currencies to generally decline, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar remained stable. However, the interest rate forecasts announced by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13-14, 2016, prompted market expectations for the US to accelerate interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to temporarily weaken thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in line with other Asian currencies, but due to the rising market expectation of the US raising interest rates in March from mid-February, the Hong Kong dollar began to show signs of weakening. During the reporting period, no exchange guarantees were triggered (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1 Exchange Rate and Fund Flow Indicator Chart 4.2 As the US dollar strengthened, the nominal effective exchange rate index for the Hong Kong dollar increased by 4.9% from August to December, and subsequently stabilized recently (Figure 4.3). Due to the minor impact of the narrowing inflation rate gap between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely follows the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Nominal and real effective exchange rate securities investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016 in Figure 4.3. The latest international balance of payments statistics show a net inflow into non-resident stock and bond securities investment in the third quarter, reflecting an improvement in global market sentiment and a large number of initial public offerings (Table 4.A). However, the outflow of large-scale debt investment by local residents, driven by the increase in US bond holdings by Hong Kong banks, has overshadowed the investment inflow from non-resident residents. Therefore, cross-border securities investment recorded a net outflow in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds showed that in the fourth quarter of 2016, there was an outflow of securities investment, mainly due to the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election, coupled with expectations of an accelerated pace of raising interest rates in the US, which put pressure on local financial markets and other Asian markets (Figure 4.4). However, the latest data shows that the Hong Kong securities investment experienced capital inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly because investors were optimistic about the US adopting expansionary fiscal policies, which improved the performance of the global financial markets. (Figure 4.4) The market survey outlook for stock and bond related fund flows indicates that fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar fund flows may increase. If the pace of interest rate normalization in the US accelerates, it will increase the risk of capital flows to the Hong Kong dollar reversing. At the same time, amid uncertainties regarding the new US government, the UK's Brexit process, and the election of EU member states, capital flows may experience increased volatility. Furthermore, the increased investment demand by mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may exert pressure on capital flows into the Hong Kong dollar. Although the initial northbound trading volume exceeded the southbound trading volume after the introduction of the Sino-HK Link in December, it is expected that the bidirectional stock investment capital flows between Mainland China and Hong Kong under this scheme will gradually increase. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and volatility in the financial markets, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remains large, and driven by the growth in debt certificates, circulating banknotes, and coins issued by the government, it is expected to rise by an additional 1.7% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.5). Due to the exchange guarantees not having been triggered, the total balance of outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds is largely maintained at the high level of 122.27 billion Hong Kong dollar. In this context, due to the issuance of foreign exchange fund notes amounting to 49 billion Hong Kong dollar to meet the bank's substantial demand for liquidity management, the total balance contracted, and correspondingly, outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds increased. Due to the gradual stabilization of the local economy, the pace of Hong Kong dollar money supply growth has accelerated. Figure 4.5 shows the components of the monetary base. The growth in the Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half of the year. As the market reassessed the inflation risk in the United States, global financial markets experienced volatility again at the beginning of the year. In February, global stock markets sharply declined from the high levels at the end of January, completely offsetting the significant gains at the beginning of the year, and the benchmark 10-year United States Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global stock markets have continued to rise in a low-volatility environment because the market anticipates an ideal state where the economic environment will continue steady growth, and inflation and interest rates remain low. However, this expectation is positive for global monetary tightening, rising trade protectionism sentiment, and tense geopolitical situations. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, and the market continues to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall lending continued to increase, but at a slower pace. The increase in property prices and transaction volume recovered in the fourth quarter of 2017 after a moderate slowdown in the previous year. Looking ahead, volatility in global and local financial markets may add fluctuation to capital flows to Hong Kong. Given the uncertainty in the financial markets, and the normalization of United States monetary policy and ongoing geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant regarding increased fluctuations in interest rates and potential risks of capital outflow. Especially, given the continuous rise in corporate leverage and the high level of personal debt burden, banks should assess the impact of interest rates increases exceeding expectations on asset quality. After the Chicago options exchange volatility index (VIX) hovered at low levels for more than two years, global financial markets resumed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global stock markets fell sharply from the high point at the end of January, with the S\&P 500 index once dropping by over 10%, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment has shifted, due to indications suggesting that the global economic recovery could put pressure on the long-low United States wages and prices, potentially leading the Federal Reserve to accelerate its interest rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year United States Treasury yield also rose to the four-year high. The global stock markets have been rising for the past two years, based on the expectation that the economic situation will remain ideal. In the second half of 2017, the growth drivers of the global economic continued to strengthen, and economic activity in advanced and emerging market economies simultaneously rebounded. As the year-end approaches, the United States Congress passed a tax reform package, which includes tax cuts and comprehensive reforms to corporate and individual tax laws, leading the market to anticipate that the United States' strong economic recovery will receive additional cyclical stimulus in the short term. Despite increased activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remains mild, further solidifying the market's expectation that global interest rates will remain low for the long term. In this context, the global asset market significantly rose in 2017, with the United States stock market in particular setting new highs repeatedly. However, with the United States releasing January wage growth data stronger than expected, global stock markets are reassessing inflation risk. After short-term fluctuations in the financial markets, the risk of global monetary tightening may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the United States, the economy has reached its potential output, and the expected cyclical stimulus from tax cuts may accelerate the inflation rebound, thereby prompting the Federal Reserve to hasten monetary policy tightening. Concurrently, as tax cuts will lead to an increase in the fiscal deficit, the United States may issue more government bonds in the future, which is expected to increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the Federal Reserve continues to pursue normalization of the balance sheet. Outside the United States, the growth momentum in other major advanced economies' economy is strengthening, leading to market expectations that their central banks may reduce the scale of quantitative easing programs. If implemented, this action will lead to a synchronized tightening of the global monetary situation. Policy and event risks arising from the tense international politics and geopolitical situation could also cast a shadow over the prospects for global economic growth. The United States government appears to be increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionist measures to shield domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of imposing import tariffs on solar panel, washing machine steel, and aluminum. These actions are worrying as to whether their trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. Furthermore, should geopolitical tensions unexpectedly escalate, it may affect global trade and exacerbate volatility in the global financial markets. Given the uncertainties in the global economic outlook, whether the currently high valuations in the global asset market can be sustained is questionable. From a fundamental level, whether the cyclical growth in global demand and expectations of United States tax cuts will lead to an increase in the fiscal deficit and consequently push up the natural interest rates (R\*) remains to be observed. The normalization of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet will lead to an increase in term premiums or push up long-term interest rates, which will be unfavorable for asset market valuations. In the Asia-Pacific region, the regional economy is in an ideal environment of steady growth and moderate inflation. With good economic performance and optimistic prospects, capital is also accelerating inflow, and the financial markets are simultaneously rising. However, due to the synchronized normalization of monetary policy by the major central banks, global liquidity is tightening. The United States government implements inward-looking trade policies. Tense geopolitical situations and the possibility of multinational corporations repatriating profits to the United States under the country's tax reform could tighten offshore dollar liquidity, and these factors all pose a downside risk to the aforementioned good prospects. Once credit and the financial markets face any shock, a reversal of capital flows is possible, and industries and economies with higher leverage are most susceptible to the impact of tightening financial conditions. In mainland China, the Chinese domestic economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by factors such as steady consumption, robust infrastructure investment, and a rebound in industrial expenditure near the end of the year. At the same time, signs of the rise of the "new economy" are becoming increasingly evident, with industries such as manufacturing and services with high added value demonstrating strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the recent economy growth prospects remain positive, but there are still uncertain factors. In particular, the extent to which the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth from further promoting structural reforms remains to be observed. The mainland authorities announced in 2018 to continue adopting an active fiscal policy stance, which may help alleviate adverse changes to the economy when necessary. During the review period, progress has been made in both structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. Specifically, with the introduction of tightening measures, the domestic real estate market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, due to banks tightening loan approval standards, the risk exposure of companies in overcapacity industries to banks remains controlled, and shadow banking activities have also slowed down in the context of financial deleveraging. In addition to the positive developments above, our analysis also indicates that the capital allocation efficiency in mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, the borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises with weaker repayment capabilities appear to have tightened, possibly due to a weakening of support provided by local governments (see Special Topic 2 on page 28 for details). Regarding external factors, under conditions of stabilizing economy trends and reduced risk, the pressure for capital outflow remained mild for most of the time in 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained a year-on-year growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Gross domestic product at local increased by 3.8% in the full year 2017, the fastest growth in nearly six years. Due to good employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Overall investment expenditure also rebounded due to increased corporate capital expenditure. Regarding external factors, benefiting from the improvement in global trade growth, coupled with the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry, Hong Kong's export performance has consequently improved further. Nevertheless, due to the faster growth rate of imports compared to exports, net exports continue to drag down the growth of local gross domestic product, while net service exports contribute positively to the growth of local gross domestic product. The expected economy growth in 2018 will remain steady. Private consumption, real estate and construction activities, and exports will continue to support the economy's growth. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will ultimately rise, Special Topic 3 will research the impact of higher mortgage repayments on private consumption. The government and market consensus forecast that the growth of the gross domestic product at local in 2018 will be between 3 to 4% and 3.0%, respectively. However, the growth prospects of Hong Kong are still affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, the economic performance of mainland China under tightening financial conditions, and the trend of the Hong Kong asset market. Although the unemployment rate has fallen to a low of 2.9% in nearly 20 years, local inflation pressure remains under control. However, the pace of inflation has shown a slight increase in the recent months on a year-on-year basis. In this, the prices of trade goods and services have all risen. Looking ahead, the core inflation rate may slightly rise to a still moderate level, partially reflecting the transmission effect brought about by the newly signed private residential rent increases. Due to the impact of the demand for capital from the new share issuance activities and seasonal capital requirements, liquidity conditions tightened, the settlement activity for short positions in the Hong Kong dollar increased, prompting the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate to strengthen from September to November 2017. As liquidity conditions have eased and interest rate hedging activities have become active again, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has weakened again since December 2017. At the beginning of 2018, despite volatility in the global financial markets (especially the stock market), the Hong Kong dollar remained largely stable. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate further weakened in early March 2018, but the conversion guarantee was not triggered. Interbank lending rates in Hong Kong dollar banks faced upward pressure from September 2017 to December 2017. This is mainly due to the capital requirements of the new share issuance activities and the cautious stance of the banks towards liquidity management at the end of the year. In December 2017, the average overnight and three-month interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks rose by 14 and 50 basis points, respectively, to 0.25% and 1.26%. Interbank lending rates among Hong Kong banks remained largely stable after a slight decline in early 2018, unaffected by recent adjustments in the global financial markets. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average loan interest rates for new mortgages from banks still followed the upward trend of interbank lending rates for Hong Kong dollar banks, rising to 2.16% in December 2017. On the other hand, the financing costs for retail banks remained generally low after a temporary rise in new share issuance activities in October, with the composite interest rates closing at 0.38% in December 2017. Looking ahead, as the United States monetary policy continues to normalize, the Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. If the Market sentiment of the global financial markets changes drastically, the volatility of capital flows may increase. In the full year of 2017, the total amount of loans from banks grew steadily by 16.1%. After a strong growth of 10.2% in the first half of the year, the loan growth rate slowed to 5.3% in the second half of the year. Among them, the growth rate of local loans and loans used outside of Hong Kong in most industries has all declined. Foreign currency loan growth is slowing, partly due to rising dollar financing costs. Due to the improvement in the local economic environment and relatively lower financing costs in the Hong Kong dollar, Hong Kong dollar loans continue to record rapid growth. Due to the growth rate of Hong Kong dollar loans being faster than deposits, the Hong Kong loan-to-deposit ratio increased in the second half of 2017, reaching 82.7% at year-end, a high since March 2015. On the other hand, due to the relatively slow growth of foreign currency loans, the foreign currency deposit ratio fell to 63.1% at year-end. The onshore and offshore RMB to USD exchange rate showed signs of stabilization from September 2017 to November 2017. Subsequently, as the USD significantly weakened against most major currencies, the onshore and offshore RMB exchange rate against the USD has strengthened since December 2017, including in February. The offshore RMB capital pool in Hong Kong (including the total amount of RMB customer deposits and time deposits) slightly recovered in the second half of the year after a slight decline in the first half, generally reflecting changes in the market's expectations for the RMB exchange rate. As for other offshore RMB businesses, although RMB lending continues to decrease, the amount of RMB trade settlements handled by Hong Kong banks has increased in the second half of the year. The average daily transaction amount of the RMB real-time payment settlement system remains high. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB businesses are expected to benefit from the promotion of the Belt and Road Initiative and the continued internationalization of the RMB.

The momentum of the global economy has remained strong since the latter part of 2016. Improving growth prospects drove global stock markets to continue rising in 2017 and early 2018. However, as the market reassessed the inflation risk in the United States, global stock markets experienced a sell-off and significant volatility in February, marking the end of two years of calm in the financial markets. Looking ahead, tightening global financial conditions, as well as a series of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global outlook. In the tight labor market, tax cuts in the United States may accelerate the cyclical rebound of inflation, prompting the Federal Reserve to hasten the tightening of monetary policy. As the Federal Reserve continues to promote balance sheet normalization, the United States' issuance of government bonds to meet tax cuts may increase upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Trade barriers and the shadow of rising geopolitical tensions, should unexpectedly intensify, could also pose a threat to the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, benefiting from strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real economic growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. However, although the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces various downside risks, such as the tightening of global monetary conditions potentially exceeding expectations, the United States' inward-looking trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. Once these downside risks occur, it will also increase the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges; on one hand, they must guard against the risks of economic growth, and on the other hand, they must limit the impact of prolonged loose monetary conditions on inflation and the vulnerability of the balance sheet. In mainland China, the economic performance in the second half of 2017 was good. During the review period, structural reforms and the containment of systemic risks have made several advancements. Recent growth prospects remain positive, but uncertainties still exist, and this will partly depend on the extent to which rapid growth in the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressure on growth from the further advancement of structural reforms. Due to the stabilization of economic conditions and the reduction of risk, the pressure for capital outflow remained mild for most of the period in 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has become increasingly solid since the latter part of 2016, the growth of advanced and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among major advanced economies, investment and exports have steadily increased, driven by the optimistic sentiment in the private sector in the United States and the significant depreciation of the dollar, while the Eurozone and Japan have also recorded a comprehensive cyclical recovery. Exports from emerging market economies also benefit from the stabilization of global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, following the tax reform in the United States, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by the reduction in corporate and individual income taxes. Given the current upward momentum in cyclical economic conditions and the expansionary effect of the United States tax reform, the International Monetary Fund predicted in January that global economy economic growth would accelerate from the 2017 estimate of approximately 3.7% to 3.9% in 2018 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: Real Gross Domestic Product growth forecasts, with the strengthening growth drivers of the Eurozone and Japan, lead to market expectations that global monetary policy divergence will narrow, coupled with more optimistic global growth prospects, stimulating risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, which in turn puts downward pressure on the dollar. Although the Federal Reserve raised interest rates three times during the year and began promoting balance sheet normalization, the dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite the comprehensive acceleration of economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remains weak and below their central bank targets, leading the market until recently to anticipate that global interest rates would remain low (Figure 2.2). In this context, global stock markets continued to rise in 2017 and early 2018, with the S\&P 500 index setting new highs, driving the cyclical adjustment in the price-to-earnings ratio to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" of the early 2000s. Figure 2.2 shows the core inflation of major advanced economies; however, since the second half of 2017, the market has been concerned that tax cuts will lead to fiscal deficits and rising inflation, causing the yield on United States government bonds to continue climbing, and whether the increasingly high valuations of asset markets can be sustained is a question. Due to the announcement of the average hourly wage growth in January 2018 in the United States being higher than expected, the market reassessed the inflation risk in the United States, triggering a adjustment in the global stock markets at the beginning of February 2018. The S&P 500 index, which experienced a drop of over 10% from its high on January 26th, completely offset the significant gains of the year and continued to be pressured after the United States government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year United States government bond yield also rose to a four-year high in February. The market volatility sharply increased, and the Chicago Options Exchange volatility index surged to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the environment of narrow fluctuations over the past two years (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 The outlook for the Chicago Options Exchange volatility index (VIX) in the future indicates that following short-term stock market volatility, inflation risk in the United States, the risk of rising long-term bond yields in the United States, and other major central banks potentially tightening monetary policy could all lead to a tightening of global monetary conditions, subsequently casting a shadow over the global economic outlook. Firstly, regarding the inflation risk in the United States, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions that are expected to provide short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The main measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and individual income tax rates, (2) temporarily allowing the full cost of capital investment to be expensed, and (3) a one-time provision to "treat as repatriated" the motivation for United States companies to keep their overseas profits offshore. Although it is not yet certain how tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, as the United States economy has now reached its potential output, tax cuts could push the United States' output beyond the potential range, subsequently leading to an overheating economy and a cyclical inflation rebound. If the magnitude of rising inflation pressure exceeds expectations, it will prompt the Federal Reserve to accelerate the tightening of monetary policy. Currently, the trajectory of the Federal Funds rate expectations in the financial markets is flatter than the forecasts issued by the Federal Reserve. However, if inflation unexpectedly rebounds, the risk of a sudden readjustment of interest rate expectations cannot be ruled out (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4 is the forecast for the Federal Funds rate; in view of the possibility that tax reform may exacerbate fiscal deficits, the issuance volume of United States government bonds is expected to increase in the future. As the Federal Reserve continues to implement the balance sheet normalization program, it is expected to lead to an increase in term premiums. In this situation, an increase in the issuance of United States government bonds may exacerbate upward pressure on long-term bond yields. Furthermore, as the market anticipates the increased possibility of the United States implementing tax cuts, inflation expectations in the United States have continued to rise since the second half of 2017 (Figure 2.5). Therefore, the benchmark 10-year United States government bond yield, after hovering at a low level for most of 2017, has risen by over 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns about increased government bond supply pressure and rising inflation expectations. Figure 2.5 five-year long-term inflation expectations, in addition, whether the natural interest rate (R\*), which is a major component of the long-term interest rate, will remain at a low level for the long term as most people expect, is a major key. Although estimates for R\* vary, it is generally believed that it has fallen significantly since the global financial crisis (Figure 2.6). Nevertheless, due to (1) the expectation of increased fiscal deficits leading to a decline in the national savings rate, and (2) corporate tax cuts and more favorable tax treatment for capital expenditures may cause the investment rate to rise, the R\* of the United States may face an upward risk in the future. An increase in R\* and expectations of Federal Reserve balance sheet normalization will lead to an increase in term premiums, potentially signaling a rise in long-term interest rates, which will pose a resistance to asset market valuations. Figure 2.6 estimates that the growth drivers for the United States R\* third, the Eurozone, and Japan have strengthened, leading the market to anticipate that their central banks may reduce monetary easing measures. Once this situation arises, it may indicate that global monetary conditions will tighten simultaneously. In the Eurozone, the economies of all member states recorded a comprehensive cyclical expansion (Figure 2.7). As for Japan, the economy is also accelerating its recovery, with the Real Gross Domestic Product recording growth for the eighth consecutive quarter in the fourth quarter of 2017. Although the European Central Bank (ECB) and the Bank of Japan continue to signal a maintenance of accommodative monetary policy amid subdued inflation, the brightening growth prospects for the Euro-Japan economy (and the continued tightening of the labor market in Japan) have led some market participants to anticipate a further reduction of quantitative easing in the near future.
