With robust local demand and improving export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained a steady growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The expected economic growth in 2018 will remain steady. Hong Kong's economic prospects remain affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, the strengthening of protectionist sentiment in global financial markets, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although domestic inflation pressure should remain mild, some upside risks still exist. The Hong Kong economy maintained growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The real local gross domestic product, adjusted for seasonal factors, grew by a quarter-on-quarter rate of 0.8% in the third and fourth quarters, which is the same as the average growth rate of 0.9% in the previous two quarters (Figure 3.1). Compared to the first half of the year, private consumption continues to grow steadily and remains one of the main drivers of local GDP growth. Consumption growth is steady, due to a good employment and income situation, continued consumer optimism, and a positive impact from rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, corporate capital expenditure increased, causing overall investment expenditure to show a significant rise in the last quarter after a relatively stable performance across the three quarters. Regarding external factors, benefiting from the improvement in global trade growth, coupled with the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry, Hong Kong's export performance has consequently improved further (Figure 3.2). Nevertheless, due to the faster growth rate of imports compared to exports, net merchandise exports continue to drag down the growth of local GDP, while net services exports contribute positively to the growth of local GDP. Figure 3.1 of the real local gross domestic product growth rate and the contribution of major expenditure items, Figure 3.2. The driving force of real import-export economic growth continues, leading to an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. The total number of employment increased by approximately 0.7% during the period to over 3.85 million, with the most significant increases in the construction, financial, and commercial services industries, as well as the public administration, social, and personal services industries. Since the growth in real local gross domestic product exceeded the growth in employment, labor productivity shows signs of further improvement. The expected economic growth in 2018 will remain steady. Regarding external factors, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from the improving global economic growth prospects and the gradual recovery of the inbound tourism industry. Locally, private consumption will continue to grow, mainly due to favorable labor market conditions. Given that the Hong Kong dollar interest rate will ultimately rise, this special study examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. Regarding locally fixed capital formation, benefiting from increased housing supply and the continued development of infrastructure projects, buildings and construction activities are expected to grow steadily. Although an improving economic environment will stimulate commercial capital expenditure, interest rates may rise or bring negative impacts. The government forecasts that the real local GDP will grow by 3 to 4% in 2018, while forecasts from international organizations and private sector analysts range from 2 to 4%. However, the growth prospects of Hong Kong are still affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the external environment, the economic performance of Mainland China under tightened financial conditions, and the trend of Hong Kong's asset market mentioned in previous chapters. Locally, domestic inflation pressure remained under control in the second half of 2017, but the year-on-year inflation momentum showed a slight uptick in recent months. Year-on-year, the Consumer Price Index rose by 1.7% in the third quarter and 1.6% in the fourth quarter, which is similar to the average increase of approximately 1.7% in the first half of that year. However, the core inflation rate, annualized over three months, reflecting the inflationary momentum, slightly increased to 2.8% in January 2018 (Figure 3.3). In this, the prices of trade goods and services have all risen. The increase in rent for newly signed private residences since mid-2016 may have also contributed to inflationary pressures to some extent (Figure 3.4). Furthermore, labor cost pressure has remained moderate over the past few quarters (Figure 3.5). Figure 3.3 reflects different indicators of consumer price inflation, Figure 3.4 shows the combined consumer price index, rental items, and market rent, and Figure 3.5 shows unit labor costs and per capita wages. Due to the still moderate global inflation and stable locally cost increases, the inflation pressure in Hong Kong is expected to remain moderate in 2018, but the core inflation rate may gradually rise from the 1.7% low of 2017. For example, due to the transmission effect brought about by the newly signed private residential rent increase, inflation pressure may increase in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate in 2018 to be a mild 2.2%, while the government forecasts the core inflation rate to be 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is mild, upside risks still exist. Regarding external factors, if global inflation or commodity prices record an increase beyond expectations, it may increase locally inflationary pressures. Regarding locally factors, the labor market has tightened further recently, and the unemployment rate, adjusted for seasonal factors, decreased from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December of the quarter in 2017, which is the first time it has been below 3% in nearly 20 years (Figure 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be near zero; if the labor market tightens significantly, it could exert additional upward pressure on inflation. Figure 3.6: After the 2008 global financial crisis, low interest rates and the unemployment rate led to an increase in mortgage debt for Hong Kong households. As the normalization of the US dollar interest rates progresses, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate will ultimately follow the rise in US dollar interest rates, and future mortgage repayment burdens for households will correspondingly increase, thereby dragging down household consumption. Therefore, this study investigates the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. Mortgage repayment burdens refer to the proportion of mortgage debt repayment (i.e., the amount of interest payments plus the principal repayment amount) to the total interest. Figure B3.1 shows the role of mortgage repayment burdens in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. Besides the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect induced by changes in asset prices mentioned in general economic theory, interest rate shocks will also affect private consumption by altering mortgage repayment burdens, subsequently changing household disposable income. This impact will expand with the increase in the outstanding mortgage loan amount. Furthermore, the principal repayment amount will fluctuate with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which will also affect private consumption by altering household disposable income. Figure B3.1 The determinants of private consumption are measured by assessing the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption; we estimated the outstanding mortgage repayment to total interest ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the mortgage repayment burdens index currently applicable only to new mortgage debt, OMDSR encompasses the total outstanding mortgage debt of all household private consumption. We roughly reference the method used by international settlement banks and use the standard formula OMDSR for fixed installment payments: where Dt is the outstanding balance of residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total interest of self-occupied households (measured by multiplying the median total interest of self-occupied households by the number of self-occupied households), and rt and st are the average interest rates and term of the outstanding mortgage loan, respectively. To assess whether OMDSR can reliably measure the entire household's mortgage repayment burdens, it is advisable to compare OMDSR with two commonly used burden indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the OMDSR estimates from 1985 to 2017, as well as the median ratio of mortgage contributions, loan repayments, and total interest estimated by the government statistics department based on quinquennial population censuses. In the early 2000s, both ratios showed a downward trend, which is consistent with the trend of decreased overall household mortgage borrowing and a significant drop in mortgage interest rates following the bursting of the property market bubble in 1997. Despite the significant rise in property prices following the global financial crisis, these two ratios remain stable due to the Monetary Authority's macroprudential measures on bank mortgage loans, which have contained overall household mortgage leverage. Furthermore, the extension of the term for new mortgage loans also reduces the actual amount of mortgage payments. Figure B3.2OMDSR and the median ratio of mortgage payments, loan repayments, and total interest; we will also compare the OMDSR with the bank's payment and interest ratio, which is the actual repayment and interest ratio for new mortgage applicants from the bank. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than the bank's loan-to-total interest ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. Because the property price was lower when the existing mortgages were established, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the mortgage repayment burdens indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., OMDSR) will be lower than the burden indicators for new mortgages (i.e., the bank's loan-to-total interest ratio) for mortgage payments. Furthermore, the bank's loan-to-total interest ratio is higher because the bank complies with the prudential supervision requirements of the Monetary Authority when calculating the bank's loan-to-total interest ratio and non-mortgage loan repayments. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and the bank's loan-to-total interest ratio remained stable, mainly due to the Monetary Authority's prudent supervision of mortgage loans, which set a ceiling on the bank's loan-to-total interest ratio, and this measure also helped to stabilize the OMDSR for Chart B3.3. The loan-to-total interest ratio for OMDSR and new mortgages by banks are generally consistent with the common burden indicators, but the OMDSR has stronger immediacy and can reflect the burden of the total outstanding mortgage debt, and not just the burden of new mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe that using OMDSR can assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. To assess the impact of mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model according to the methods of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016) for mortgage payments and mortgages. Among these, the relationship between actual private consumption (measured by the actual average private consumption per household) and its long-term determinants is presented in the short term formula as an error-correction term. Based on existing theories and empirical evidence, real income (measured by the median of household total interest, deflated by the combined consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (measured by housing prices and the Hang Seng Index, deflated by the combined consumer price index), and OMDSR are long-term determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, and the local banking industry continues to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, the total loan amount continued to increase, but the growth rate slowed compared to the first half of the year. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy continues to normalize, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate may face greater upward pressure. If global financial market sentiment changes drastically, the volatility of capital flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the spot exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Figure 4.1). The spot exchange rate for the Hong Kong dollar temporarily strengthened and remained around 7.80 during the period from September to November 2017. This is mainly due to the increased funding demand from new share issuance activities and the banks' cautious stance on liquidity management before the end of the month and year, leading to a tightening of liquidity conditions, which in turn caused the slowing down of interest rate arbitrage activities and an increase in the settlement of Hong Kong dollar short positions. As the situation of Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased, and with rising commercial demand for the US dollar at year-end, the spot exchange rate for the Hong Kong dollar softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in the global financial market (especially the stock market), the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the exchange rate of Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar weakened, but the conversion guarantee was not triggered (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and Figure 4.2 capital flows indicators: The nominal effective exchange rate index for the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Figure 4.3). This is largely consistent with the trend of the US dollar against most major currencies. Due to the small difference in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trading partners and the limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continues to closely track the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3 shows the inflow of securities investments by non-local residents in nominal and real effective exchange rate during the second half of 2017. The latest international balance of payments statistics show an inflow of stock investment for both local and non-local residents in the third quarter, reflecting an improving economic outlook in the region and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt securities investments by non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, offsetting outflows of debt investments by local residents. A survey of global mutual funds also indicated that due to the market's optimistic outlook on economic prospects and corporate earnings, equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017 in recent weeks; the survey data showed that despite adjustments in the global financial market, equity investments still recorded inflows, while bond investments recorded slight capital flows out (Figure 4.4). Figure 4.4 survey outlook for capital flows related to equity and bonds in the market indicates that as the US monetary policy normalization process continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, potentially leading to an increase in hedging activities. Therefore, the possibility that the Hong Kong dollar swap arrangement will be triggered should not be excluded. This is a normal process under the pegged exchange rate system. Meanwhile, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalization is not yet clear, and global macroeconomic financial conditions and market sentiment are volatile, fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar capital flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to fully ensure the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate according to the mechanism of the Currency Board. Despite the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and ongoing balance sheet reduction, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The Hong Kong dollar currency base rose by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, mainly due to the growth in debt certificates issued by the issuance of banknotes (Figure 4.5). Due to the exchange guarantee not being triggered, the total balance of the surplus and outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds for the second half of the year will remain essentially unchanged at approximately 1226.8 billion Hong Kong dollar. The total balance has decreased, while outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds have correspondingly increased. This is due to the issuance of foreign exchange fund notes (totaling 80 billion Hong Kong dollar) to meet the substantial demand of banks in liquidity management. Entering 2018, despite market adjustments, the currency base remained stable. The components of the currency base in Figure 4.5, at the same time, the supply of Hong Kong dollar currency further increased in the second half of 2017, but the growth rate slowed. The growth in Hong Kong dollar money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half of the year to 2.5% in the second half of the year. As a main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased slightly by 2.2% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half of the year, partly due to a booming asset market and rising investment demand. Asset analysis corresponding shows that the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 is supported on one hand by the strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Figure 4.6), and on the other hand, it is dragged down by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from non-bank private sectors and the contraction of net foreign exchange assets in the banks. Regarding the changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its corresponding asset, foreign currency deposit growth has been mixed. Figure 4.6 Some reflect the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, and the growth rate of US dollar deposits decreased from 3.0% in the first half of the year to 2.4% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits continued to fall for over two years before showing a significant rebound in the second half of the year, with an increase of 8.4%. This is mainly driven by the recent rebound in RMB deposits. Due to the slowdown in the growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits, the total deposits of institutions in the second half of the year increased slightly by 3.0%, while the growth rate in the first half of the year was 5.6%. For the full year 2017, the total deposit amount grew moderately by 8.7%, which was roughly the same as in 2016. Figure 4.7, during the period from September to December 2017, the funding demand for new share issuance activities increased, while banks maintained a cautious stance on liquidity management before the end of the month and year-end, which put upward pressure on interbank lending rates in the Hong Kong dollar banking sector (Figure 4.8). Compared to six months ago, overnight and three-month Hong Kong banks' interbank rates rose by 14 and 50 basis points, respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (calculated as the monthly average). The negative interest rate differential on interbank rates for Hong Kong dollar and US dollar banks for one-month to three-month periods has also narrowed accordingly. Figure 4.8 shows that Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank rates are moving in tandem; at the same time, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve is shifting upwards but becoming flatter, with a trend largely similar to the movement of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half of the year, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by 63 basis points, closing at 1.52% at year-end of 2017, while the increase in the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds was smaller, rising by 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at year-end of 2017 (Figure 4.9). Figure 4.9, the comprehensive interest rates for government bonds and the average loan interest rate for new mortgages entered 2018, and the Hong Kong dollar banks and peer market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand decreased, interbank rates in the Hong Kong dollar banks fell in early January. Subsequently, despite adjustments in global and local market, interbank rates in the Hong Kong dollar banks sector remained largely stable. The overnight and three-month Hong Kong banks interbank rates were 0.43% and 1.08%, respectively, at the end of February 2018. Regarding the retail sector, although bank lending rates have risen in line with the increase in Hong Kong banks' interbank rates, the banks' financing costs generally remain low due to the substantial deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages by banks gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Figure 4.9), largely following the upward trend in the interbank rates of Hong Kong banks for one month. On the other hand, the composite interest rate for retail banks' Hong Kong dollar financing costs, although temporarily increased in October due to increased funding demand from new share issuance activities, remained relatively soft for most of the second half of the year, closing at 0.38% at the end of the month. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy continues to normalize, and other major economies may initiate interest rate normalization, the Hong Kong dollar interest rate may face greater upward pressure. Simultaneously, fluctuations in global market sentiment and rapid changes in the macroeconomic financial situation may increase the volatility of capital flows. However, the large Hong Kong dollar currency base can serve as a buffer, helping to mitigate a rapid rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Furthermore, prudent liquidity management by banks and discounting through a discount window also help to curb excessive fluctuations in interbank rates. Credit from banks grew strongly throughout the full year of 2017. The loan growth rate reached 10.2% in the first half of the year, slowing to 5.3% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.10); the growth in loans used in Hong Kong and loans used outside of Hong Kong in the second half of 2017 both slowed down. According to currency analysis, due to the improving local economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar financing costs, Hong Kong dollar loans will continue to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans will only slightly increase by 0.1%. Among them, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to the rise in US dollar financing costs. In the full year of 2017, the total loan amount recorded a strong growth of 16.1%, while in 2016 it was 6.5% for the loans. The growth rate of loans used in Hong Kong (including trade finance) for Figure 4.10 decreased from 9.4% in the first half of the year to 5.6% in the second half of the year, with performance varying across major industries (Figure 4.11). The growth rate of loans for the construction industry, property development, and investment slowed in the second half of the year, partly because, since June 2017, the authorities have required banks to strengthen risk management for loans to property developers. Although commodity trade and retail sales improved further, loans in the trade finance and transportation sectors recorded only a relatively slight increase, while loans in the wholesale and retail sectors recorded a decline. Conversely, the growth in loans for financial and financial-related enterprises remains strong, which to some extent reflects the steady expansion of the financial services industry. Figure 4.11 shows that the growth in local loans for individual industries and household debt in the second half of 2017 increased by 6.5%, while the growth in the first half of the year was 5.0%. Within household debt, private loans (including credit card advances and other private purpose loans) have further accelerated growth, reaching a 12.4% increase in the second half of the year. The strong growth of private loans is mainly driven by lending from private banks that use financial assets as collateral and from wealth management clients. The growth of these loans is roughly commensurate with the continuous growth of the client assets managed by the banks. The risk of this type of mortgage loans is within a controllable range. Furthermore, in January 2014, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority issued guidance to banks on private loans risk management, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting limits on loan tenors and borrower repayment ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volume has increased, the loan-to-value ratio for new mortgages has fallen, and the growth rate of residential mortgage loans slightly declined to 3.8% in the second half of the year. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Figure 4.12).

Primarily benefiting from the increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared to the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity position remains stable. Credit growth experienced strong growth in the first half of 2017, but slowed in the second half, while asset quality remains robust when measured against historical standards. Although interbank lending rates in Hong Kong have risen significantly, due to low retail deposit interest rates, the cost of Hong Kong funding for retail banks remains at a low level. However, banks should be vigilant against the risks of widening interest rate fluctuations and potential capital outflows under the normalization of U.S. monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Due to the continuous increase in corporate leverage, personal debt burdens are also at a high level, and banks should assess the impact of interest rate hikes exceeding expectations on asset quality. To enhance the ability of banks to withstand systemic risk, the ratio of countercyclical buffer capital in Hong Kong will be increased to 2.5% starting from January 1, 2019. In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% compared to the same period last year. This is primarily benefited by the significant increase in net interest income and the reduction in loan impairment provisions, which is sufficient to offset the decrease in non-interest income. However, due to asset growth outpacing earnings growth, in the second half of 2017, the return on assets for retail banks slightly decreased from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15%. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than 1.11% in the same period of 2016 (Figure 5.1). For the full year 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Figure 5.1 Retail bank profitability: The net interest margin for retail banks expanded from 1.34% in the same period of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Figure 5.2). Evidence suggests that the improvement in the net interest margin is consistent with the rise in the average interest rate spread for Hong Kong corporate loans in the syndicated loan market (Figure 5.3). Figure 5.2 shows the net interest margin of retail banks, and Figure 5.3 shows the average spread for Hong Kong dollar syndicated loans. Since September 2017, interbank lending rates among banks in Hong Kong have risen across the board, mainly driven by the demand for liquidity related to the initial public offering and the liquidity needs of banks near the end of the year, as well as expectations of interest rate hikes in the U.S. Among these, the 3-month interbank lending rates of banks in Hong Kong recorded a high of 1.31% at the end of December 2017 following the financial crisis, an increase of 53 basis points from the end of June, but when measured against historical standards, it remains at a lower level (blue line in Figure 5.4). Entering 2018, due to a easing of year-end liquidity demands from the banks, interbank lending rates among banks in Hong Kong appeared to have stabilized. Although interbank lending rates among banks in Hong Kong have recently risen, the cost of Hong Kong funding for retail banks remains stable. This is mainly due to the low retail deposit interest rates during the review period. In this situation, the composite interest rate reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks remained at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, only slightly rising to the 0.38% level at the end of December. (The green line in Figure 5.4). The overall HKD and USD funding costs for licensed banks in Hong Kong have also shown a similar situation. In the second half of 2017, the average funding costs for non-deposit markets in the banks rose by 35 basis points in HKD and USD, while the average deposit funding costs rose slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total funding costs for licensed banks in HKD and USD increased by 22 basis points (red line in Figure 5.5). In the second half of 2018, the global economy maintained growth. However, although the United States economy is growing steadily, the growth momentum in other regions is slowing down. The slowdown in global trade and the significant drop in oil prices both pose cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. Given the slowdown in global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points, respectively, from the October 2018 forecasts in January. Due to the weakening growth prospects and rising trade friction, global stock markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The United States Treasury yield curve has flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, raising market concerns that the United States is about to face a recession. Regarding the United States, although moderate inflation provides the Federal Reserve room to pause interest rate hikes, the Federal Reserve's policy tends to be data-dependent, also suggesting that the financial markets may be more sensitive to future data releases, especially data that could prompt tighter monetary policy, such as increases in United States inflation. Meanwhile, the results of trade negotiations between the United States and China, as well as between the United States and the European Union, remain unclear. Due to the significant contraction in shadow financing activities, the financing difficulties faced by private enterprises (especially small companies) over the past few quarters have increased, and the weakening of economy confidence may also exert pressure on business activities. During the review period, the global economy maintained growth, but the growth momentum weakened under the combined influence of specific and cyclical headwinds, particularly in regions outside the United States. Given the softening growth prospects, the Federal Reserve is adjusting its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions will be "data-dependent" and require "patience," and is no longer providing forward guidance on further rate hikes. Due to the Federal Reserve's policy leaning being data-dependent, financial markets may be more sensitive to future data releases, and monetary policy may become more uncertain. At the same time, as uncertainties in global trade policy and heightened geopolitical risks intensify, they may continue to cast a shadow over the prospects for the global economy. In the Asia-Pacific region, due to signs of a slowdown in the United States' rate hikes cycle, coupled with the stabilization of the dollar, the financial markets have been relatively stable since the end of 2018. However, due to the deterioration of the external environment, namely the unresolved US-China trade conflict and the weakening growth of advanced economies, the region may face a comprehensive slowdown. In mainland China, the growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, and under the circumstances of the US-China trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises, the uncertainty of growth prospects increased. Therefore, policymakers are taking more targeted measures to stabilize the economy and support private and small businesses. Faced with these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to control systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow comprehensively. However, although the United States economy remains generally stable, some signs of slowdown have appeared. There are also clear signs indicating a slowdown in growth momentum in regions outside the United States. Some shocks related to specific countries, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new automobile emission standards in Germany, the sharp rise in Italian government bond yields due to the fiscal deadlock with the EU, and social unrest in France, have all dragged down the economic activity of advanced economies (Figure 2.1). Furthermore, the cyclical slowdown in global imports poses a drag on industrial production in emerging market economies (Figure 2.2). The sharp decline in oil prices in the fourth quarter also poses new challenges to the export of commodities for emerging market economies. Given the slowdown in growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth forecast for 2019 by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Due to the slowdown in global growth momentum, increasing uncertainty in trade policies, market concerns about the sustainability of corporate earnings growth in the United States, and statements by the Federal Reserve indicating that monetary policy would continue to tighten, caused significant adjustments in global stock markets. As sentiment in the financial markets deteriorates, the United States Treasury yield curve has flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, raising concerns among some market participants that the United States is about to face a recession (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 shows the spread between the 10-year and 3-month United States Treasury yields and the probability of a recession in the United States; nevertheless, the probability of a recession in the United States in the short term is very low. At the same time, the estimated output gap in the United States only regained positive values last year, making the possibility of the Federal Reserve significantly tightening monetary policy due to an overheating economy less likely. However, considering the significant tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, Federal Reserve senior officials began emphasizing that monetary policy will be data-dependent in early January, and pointed out that moderate inflationary pressure allows them to maintain "patience" when determining future monetary policy adjustments. Furthermore, after the Federal Open Market Committee of the United States held a meeting in January, it did not provide forward guidance on further rate hikes and announced that it "will consider adjusting any details of the normalization of the balance sheet in response to changes in economic and financial conditions." To reduce policy errors, the Federal Reserve increasingly emphasizes that its decisions will be data-dependent as a risk management strategy. Based on this, it is inferred that the financial markets may be more sensitive to future data releases, especially data that may prompt a tightening of monetary policy. The monetary policies of other major central banks are also unclear. Regarding the Eurozone, the European Central Bank will terminate its asset purchase programme in December, while continuing to reinvest the full principal of securities that have matured under the asset purchase programme, and reiterating its forward guidance to keep policy interest rates unchanged at least until the summer of 2019. However, the European Central Bank downgraded its short-term growth outlook in January, describing the risk to the growth prospects as "leaning downwards." The impact of the European Central Bank's recent lowering of the economic growth forecast on monetary policy remains to be observed. Regarding Japan, the central banks of Japan stated at their recent policy meeting that, in the event of increased downside risks, they will ease their monetary policy stance when necessary. However, there may be significant resistance to further easing of monetary policy, as its effectiveness is questioned, and the drawbacks of maintaining a prolonged ultra-low interest rate environment are increasingly evident, for example, due to low yields continuously dragging down profitability, the capital adequacy ratio of regional banks has fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. Therefore, the space for the central banks of Japan to adjust monetary policy in the short term is very limited. In addition to uncertainties related to the outlook for global monetary policy, uncertain trade negotiation outcomes and escalating geopolitical risks are also two major sources of risk facing the global economy. The United States government announced at the beginning of December that it would not increase tariffs on goods imported from China within 90 days, and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether both sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be observed. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the United States and the EU have made little progress at this stage. Due to the uncertain outcome of these trade negotiations, they may continue to cast a shadow over the prospects of the global economy. Policy and geopolitical risks are also quite prominent. Although the impact of the standstill on economic growth should be temporary, the strained relationship between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives may lead to further policy gridlock in the future. Regarding the UK, after the Brexit referendum bill was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, the risks associated with Brexit and its ripple effects have escalated, and whether a plan can be formulated at the last minute to avoid a destructive "hard Brexit" remains uncertain. In other regions, the geopolitical situation in the Middle East is tense, such as the United States re-sanctioning Iran, which may also constitute an uncertain factor for oil prices, thereby affecting global growth prospects. In the Asia-Pacific region, after fluctuations in the financial markets during the first three quarters of last year, they have largely stabilized in the fourth quarter. The dollar has stabilized since October, and there are indications that the Federal Reserve will remain patient regarding further rate hikes, easing the pressure of currency depreciation and capital outflow faced by economies in the Asia-Pacific region. On the other hand, if the US-China trade friction eases, leading to the locally economy performing better than expected, it may push up local inflation. Figure 3.6 shows the escalation of the unemployment rate amid the US-China trade conflict in the second half of 2018: the United States imposed 25% tariffs on imports from mainland China worth $34 billion and $16 billion on July 6 and August 23, respectively. Following these two measures, mainland China also imposed a 25% tariff on equivalent United States goods in response. The United States further increased tariffs of 10% on goods imported from mainland China valued at $200 billion on September 24. mainland China immediately imposed tariffs of 5 to 10% on United States goods valued at 60 billion US dollars in response. Subsequently, the two countries will engage in negotiations to avoid further imposition of tariffs. Since Hong Kong has always been a transshipment port between these two economies, the imposition of additional tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the US-China trade dispute has significant implications for the macroeconomic and financial stability of Hong Kong. This study reviews the recent performance of goods trade in Hong Kong and explores its short-term prospects. We will also attempt to utilize more granular data to distinguish the trade goods directly affected by the imposition of tariffs, thereby more closely examining the impact of the imposed tariffs. To analyze the impact of tariffs, we first extract data for six sets of goods transshipped through Hong Kong, which are affected by the successive rounds of the imposition of tariffs mentioned in the previous section. In the first two rounds of the imposition of tariffs, the United States primarily imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, while mainland China primarily imposed tariffs on agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the scope of affected goods has expanded, including more consumer products. For simplicity, goods affected by the imposition of tariffs in these three rounds will be named List 1, List 2, and List 3. After collecting this more detailed trade data, we will concentrate on analyzing the year-on-year changes in the turnover of transshipment cargo in Hong Kong to adjust for the impact of seasonal factors. Furthermore, readers should exercise caution when analyzing the data for September 2018, as trade activities during that month were to some extent disrupted by the super typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analysis results of this section should only be considered preliminary evidence of the impact of the imposition of tariffs. Shortly after the imposition of tariffs on goods originating in mainland China and affected by tariffs in Hong Kong, the related goods from mainland China transshipped through Hong Kong to the United States appear to have significantly decreased or slowed their growth (Figure B3.1). For example, the growth in transit for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the imposition of tariffs, while the transit for List 3 recorded negative growth. Furthermore, the turnover for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Figure B3.1 shows that the value of goods originating in the United States, passing through Hong Kong to mainland China and subject to tariffs, compared to the Hong Kong turnover of goods originating in the United States, passing through Hong Kong to mainland China, showed varying performance (Figure B3.2) in 2018. The turnover in List 1 appears to have significantly decreased within a few months after the imposition of tariffs, but has rebounded near the end of the year. The turnover for List 2 was generally at a level of negative growth for the full-year, while the growth for List 3 appears to be relatively stable. Figure B3.2 The value of goods originating from the United States, turnover transshipped through Hong Kong to mainland China in 2018 that were front-loaded due to the time lag between the announcement and final imposition of tariffs (or due to the threat of the imposition of tariffs) may have been shipped before the expected tariff effective date. In fact, some data and news reports indicate that these early shipment practices are quite common. Some private sector analysts also believe that these actions are part of the reason for the strong overall trade figures before the imposition of tariffs. More detailed trade data indicates that certain goods on the tariffs list showed signs of early shipments, but this appears to only involve goods with a turnover from mainland China to the United States (Figure B3.1). The growth in transit rate for List 1 and List 2 increased in the months preceding the enactment of their respective tariffs. On the other hand, the growth rate of turnover from the United States through Hong Kong to mainland China (Figure B3.2) does not indicate any significant early shipment practices by companies. It is noteworthy that Hong Kong turnover unaffected by the imposition of tariffs, while Hong Kong turnover (value) directly affected by the imposition of tariffs, accounts for only about 4 to 5% of the total Hong Kong turnover. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine the turnover unaffected by the imposition of tariffs. We found that the turnover in the last two months of 2018, unaffected by the imposition of tariffs, recorded negative growth (Figure B3.3). Furthermore, the growth in transit affected by tariffs (red line) has shown a significantly larger decline starting from the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs on the turnover. The slowdown in growth in turnover, unaffected by the imposition of tariffs, is partly reflecting weaker peripheral demand. As trade friction continues to lead to increased uncertainties, tightening global financial conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, peripheral demand is likely to be more broadly pressured. Especially as trade conflicts have dragged down global economic sentiment and activity, this is reflected in the adjustments in major stock markets. Import demand in other economies is thus dragged down, suppressing the performance of Hong Kong's foreign trade. Figure B3.3 The turnover of transshipment cargo in Hong Kong in 2018 still faces challenges for the short-term prospects of Hong Kong's goods trade even if the US-China trade friction eases. Global growth may slow down in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which will further suppress the performance of Hong Kong's exports. Indicators of the business climate across all sectors show that enterprises of all sizes and scales are pessimistic about their business prospects (Figure B3.4), with the trade industry's business climate being particularly sluggish. Other industries related to trade, such as logistics, may also be affected. (Figure B3.4) Survey of Business Prospects in the Hong Kong import and exports industry

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting liquidity tightening driven by anticipated seasonal funding demands, which led to the unwinding of interest rate swaps. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened due to funds repatriated by companies from new share capital and the market re-establishing positions in interest rate swaps, triggering a weakening exchange rate guarantee in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar transactions remain smooth and orderly. Hong Kong interbank lending rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demands, subsequently falling in January 2019. Looking ahead, facing uncertain factors such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, the UK Brexit negotiations, and the pace of normalization of US monetary policy, the flow of funds in the Hong Kong dollar may be more volatile. If the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar remains significantly wide, interest arbitrage activities may continue, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for a period in the future and potentially trigger a weakening exchange rate guarantee again, which is consistent with the design of the pegged exchange rate system. After the weakening exchange rate guarantee was triggered in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weakening exchange rate guarantee again four times in total in March 2019 (as of March 19) (Figure 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate temporarily rose in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of interest rate swaps amid tightening liquidity, but it gradually declined in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilized again after November, which was due to year-end funding demands driving liquidity tightening, leading to the settlement of interest rate swaps. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partially reflecting funds repatriated by companies from new share capital and the market re-establishing positions in interest rate swaps. Due to the widening of the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar after the year-end, it triggered arbitrage activities by market participants buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, driving the gradual weakening of the Hong Kong dollar, and the weakening exchange rate guarantee was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weakening exchange rate guarantee, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued smoothly and orderly. Total reserves have remained at approximately HK$76 billion since August (Figure 4.2); after the weakening exchange rate guarantee was triggered in March, it slightly decreased to HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). The funds flowing out in Hong Kong dollar since April 2018 account for only a small portion of the approximately ten trillion Hong Kong dollars that have flowed in since 2008. Figure 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Figure 4.2 Fund flow indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally follows the movement of the US dollars and continues to rise during the review period (Figure 4.3). Due to the small difference in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar is limited, and the trend of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index generally follows that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. The latest international balance of payments statistics for nominal and real effective exchange rates in Figure 4.3 show that securities investment continued to outflow in the third quarter of 2018. Amid weak market sentiment and increased stock market volatility, the outflow of securities investment by local residents accelerated, offsetting the inflow of securities investment from non-local residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investment by local residents and non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, facing uncertain factors such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, the UK Brexit negotiations, and the pace of normalization of US monetary policy, the flow of funds may intensify volatility. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and US dollars will stimulate arbitrage trading activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the pegged exchange rate system, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken, which could also trigger the weakening exchange rate guarantee. Capital outflows and the triggering of a weakening exchange rate guarantee are both normal operations under the pegged exchange rate system. Despite the ongoing normalization of US interest rates and the weakening exchange rate guarantee being triggered multiple times from April to August, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The Hong Kong dollar basis a slight decrease of 0.7% in the second half of the year, reaching HK$163.29 billion at the end of 2018 (Figure 4.4). The reduction in the currency base was mainly due to the weakening exchange rate guarantee triggered in August 2018, which caused the Total reserves to decrease from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while debt certificates, government-issued circulating banknotes and coins, outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds slightly increased. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained relatively stable during the first two months of 2019, and the Total reserves have shown no significant change since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weakening exchange rate guarantee in March, the total reserves slightly decreased to approximately HK$70.9 billion Hong Kong dollar (as of March 19). Figure 4.4, regarding the components of the monetary base and the broader indicator of Hong Kong dollar money supply, the growth rate of the money supply generally slowed in the second half of the year, reflecting an increase in uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. The Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year and only increased slightly by 0.1% in the second half of the year (Figure 4.5). As a main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits showed little change compared to the end of June (Figure 4.6). In Hong Kong dollar deposits, both current accounts and savings deposits have declined, partly due to a decrease in investment-related transactions in the second half of the year. On the other hand, due to the increase in deposit interest rates, time deposits continue to record strong growth. Asset analysis shows that due to changes in bank capital and reserves (including "net amount of other items"), the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 has slowed. Figure 4.5 the growth rate of M3 in Hong Kong dollar and corresponding asset changes in foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half of the year. Due to the increase in deposits attracted by the higher deposit interest rates on US dollars by banks, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half of the year, thus becoming the main driving factor for the growth in foreign currency deposits (Figure 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased slightly by 1.4% in the second half of the year, with RMB deposits continuing to grow. Overall, the total deposits of recognition institutions grew by 3.3% in the second half of the year, slightly faster than the 1.6% growth in the first half of the year. Figure 4.6 Although the Hong Kong dollar monetary base and deposit scale remain substantial, Hong Kong bank interbank lending rates began to face certain upward pressure in the second half of the year, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal fluctuations in liquidity demand occasionally push up short-term interbank lending rates, causing them to fluctuate more than long-term interbank lending rates (Figure 4.7). The average Hong Kong interbank lending rates for 3 months and 12 months in December were 2.32% and 2.74%, respectively, a rise of approximately 30 basis points compared to the average in June. Entering 2019, due to the decline in seasonal demand, interbank lending rates at the Hong Kong bank fell overall. The average Hong Kong interbank lending rates for 3 months and 12 months fell to 1.65% and 2.39% in February, respectively. Figure 4.7 The Hong Kong dollar and US dollars interbank lending rates yield curves declined in the second half of the year, generally following the changes in the US dollar yield curve. Compared to the end of June 2018, the yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bonds fell by 45 and 37 basis points, respectively, to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Figure 4.8). During the review period for government bond yields, composite interest rates, and average new mortgage lending rates, the composite interest rate measuring the average Hong Kong dollar financing cost of retail banks slightly increased. (Figure 4.8) Reflecting changes in the cost of banking peers and deposit financing, the composite interest rates rose from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, and subsequently fell to 0.83% at the beginning of 2019 (Figure 4.8). Given the rise in financing costs, following the upward adjustment of the US Federal Funds Rate target range in September, retail banks will increase their most favorable loan rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the target range for the US Federal Funds Rate was raised again in December, retail banks did not adjust the most favorable loan rates again. On the other hand, the average new mortgage lending rates followed the most favorable loan rates upward, approximately 2.45% at the end of 2019. Looking ahead, the trend in US dollars interest rates, capital flows, and local financial market activities (such as new share subscription activities) will continue to be the main driving factors for the Hong Kong dollar interest rate. Given that the Hong Kong dollar monetary base remains substantial, and the banking system holds a large volume of foreign exchange fund notes, as banks can use foreign exchange fund notes as collateral to borrow Hong Kong dollar funds through the discounting window, the pace of the rise in the Hong Kong dollar interest rate should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating US-China trade friction, the exchange rates of offshore RMB and onshore RMB have depreciated against the US dollars since early 2018 (Figure 4.9). However, under the optimistic sentiment driven by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the United States, the exchange rates for offshore RMB and onshore RMB stabilized in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore RMB and offshore RMB was not significant during the review period. Figure 4.9 shows that the ongoing US-China trade friction has not yet had a significant impact on the funding situation of offshore banking peers in the onshore RMB and offshore RMB exchange rates. Due to the liquidity situation remaining largely stable, the overnight offshore RMB Hong Kong interbank lending rates were below 4% for most of the review period, with occasional increases influenced by seasonal factors (Figure 4.10). The three-month offshore RMB repo rate hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, and subsequently fell to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, which may reflect the People's Bank of China's recent monetary easing measures. The growth in RMB customer deposits and deposit certificate balances was slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half of the year, growing by 3.7% in the second half of the year to RMB 657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Figure 4.11 and Table 4.B). Primarily benefiting from increased net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared to the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity conditions remain stable. Reflecting the upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank lending rates and retail deposit rates in line with the normalization of US interest rates, the overall Hong Kong dollar funding costs for retail banks have risen significantly, but remain at a low level. Amidst an uncertain external environment, bank lending experienced a moderate contraction in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilization since November, and asset quality remains sound when measured against historical standards. Looking ahead, due to the persistent uncertainty in U.S.-China trade relations, the slowdown in the global economy, the unclear pace of the tightening cycle in U.S. monetary policy, and geopolitical risks, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple obstacles.
