The coronavirus pandemic that erupted in early 2020 simultaneously impacted demand and supply, posing a challenge to the global economy unlike previous crises. Although the main central banks and some governments have launched stimulus measures since early March to curb the economic impact of the epidemic, financial markets remain volatile, and the global financial situation has also tightened. Although there are unclear factors in the external and local environments, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and currency markets continue to operate smoothly and orderly. Given the stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, stable total reserves, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of Hong Kong dollars or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the period under review. The total loan amount experienced a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, followed by a slowdown in growth in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, but the trend has been somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the COVID-19 spread situation, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continuous increase in corporate leverage and personal debt burden, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolio under conditions where these risk factors may be exacerbated. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economy growth has initially shown signs of stability, benefiting from major central banks increasing the vigor of monetary easing policies, the easing of trade tensions between China and the United States, and the reduction in the risk of a "no-deal Brexit" in the United Kingdom. However, since late January, the number of global COVID-19 infections has been continuously increasing, causing market concern and triggering significant fluctuations in the global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks have significantly cut interest rates and increased liquidity tools, while some governments have also introduced measures to support the real economy. However, under the rise in credit spreads and the sharp decline in the stock market, the global financial situation has tightened. Looking ahead, the downside risks to the global economy outlook have increased. The COVID-19 pandemic will impact the global economy, and the extent of the economic impact will depend on the severity and persistence of the pandemic. In the medium term, the relationship between the United States and its main trading partners may become tense again, and trade negotiations with the European Union after the United Kingdom's withdrawal may also face significant difficulties. Weak global demand continues to drag down economic growth in the East Asian region. Exports to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and inland China in the East Asian region remained weak in the second half of the year in 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently announced increased earnings, but whether the technology product cycle will broadly rebound remains to be observed. The financial markets reacted positively to the first phase of the US-China trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce to some extent reduced uncertainties in global trade. Nevertheless, the East Asian region will continue to face adverse factors such as weak corporate profitability and high private sector leverage ratios. At the same time, the outbreak of COVID-19 has raised concerns that the regional economy may face further pressure amid continued sluggish growth. Travel bans implemented by multiple economies in the region may harm the Asian tourism industry, especially economies that are more dependent on tourism service exports. Due to the close relationship between the regional supply chain and inland China, the manufacturing industry may also be affected by the outbreak of the epidemic. As for inland China, due to weak domestic and external demand, economic growth continued to slow down in the second half of the year of 2019. Looking ahead, although the first phase of the China-US trade agreement helps temporarily reduce the external uncertainties facing the domestic economy, downward pressure still exists in the face of the outbreak of COVID-19, continued economic rebalancing, and the slowdown of the global economy. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 will prioritize economic stability as the focus for 2020 while simultaneously emphasizing the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that China's economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small and medium-sized private enterprises. Despite relevant measures, some media reports and market analysts point out that private sector industrial enterprises may be facing a decline in shareholder equity in recent years, which is seen as a sign of a "retreat of the private sector." Special Topic 2, through a study of 2018 listed company data on the driving factors of changes in the interests of inland industrial enterprises, found that private enterprises or small enterprises are not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or "regression." Although research findings indicate negative earnings are the biggest driving factor, other factors, especially structural factors, are also worth noting (see Special Topic 2 for details). Hong Kong's economic activity significantly contracted in the second half of the year of 2019. Real Gross Domestic Product has continued to decline over the past three quarters, indicating that Hong Kong's economy has entered a recession. Affected by this drag, the economy contracted by 1.2% in 2019, which was worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marked the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in local demand, especially the contraction in private consumption, is the main factor dragging down the gross domestic product of the local area in the second half of the year of 2019. Local social events severely impact consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook and subsequently reducing consumer and business confidence. With the renewed intensification of China-US trade friction, the slowdown in global economy growth, and the severe regression in the tourism industry visiting Hong Kong, Hong Kong's foreign trade performance continues to languish. Given that the economy faced significant obstacles, the governments launched multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures from August to December 2019. To allow the banks greater space to increase support for the local economy and to help mitigate the economic cycle, the Monetary Authority announced on October 14 that the countercyclical buffer ratio for banks would be lowered from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 to 300 billion Hong Kong dollar to businesses, especially small enterprises. The economy's performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the epidemic has recently brought considerable downside risk. Since the retail, accommodation services, catering services, tourism, and transportation industries have not yet recovered after the damage caused by social events, the epidemic will bring a dual blow to these industries. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 fiscal budget proposal can provide assistance to households and businesses (especially small enterprises), including the distribution of a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for businesses under the "small enterprises financing guarantee scheme." On March 16, 2020, the Monetary Authority further lowered the countercyclical buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will allow banks greater room to intensify support for the local economy, especially for industries and individuals who are under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the epidemic. Analyzing by components of the gross domestic product of the local area, due to fragile consumption and business confidence, private consumption and investment may continue to weaken. Although governments' consumption will support economic growth, with the completion of some major infrastructure projects, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued. Regarding external factors, the initial phase of the China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, the weakness in global economy growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's foreign trade performance. Especially the outbreak of COVID-19 may lead to disruptions in the local supply chain and a slowdown in cross-border economic activity (such as the tourism industry), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance in the economy. Governments forecast that the Real Gross Domestic Product of the local area for 2020 will grow between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the slowdown in global economy growth, US-China trade relations, the economy's performance in inland China, and local social events. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of the year of 2019 and the beginning of 2020, with a decrease in the total number of employed persons, a rise in the unemployment rate, and a year-on-year decline in the real wage index. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partially reflecting the impact of social events and the epidemic on the retail, accommodation, and catering services industries. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the outbreak of COVID-19, the unemployment rate will climb further in the economy. Special Topic 3 will explore in greater detail the recent developments and short-term prospects of the labor market. Local inflation pressure continued to accumulate until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices. Subsequent economic activity weakened, and inflationary pressures also gradually eased in the economy. Due to a weak economy, stabilizing private housing rents, and moderate import inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the short term. The market consensus forecast for the overall inflation rate in 2020 will be between 0.6% and 3.7%, and the governments forecast the core inflation rate to be 2.5%. Supported by increased demand for the Hong Kong dollar related to stocks (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been further strengthened, partly due to the robust activity in initial public offerings, and partly because liquidity tightening near the end of the year prompted short positions in the Hong Kong dollar to be closed. After the Lunar New Year holiday, the liquidity situation has eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate slightly weakened towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued smoothly and orderly during the review period, and no exchange guarantees were triggered. Total reserves remain stable at approximately 54 billion Hong Kong dollar. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar bank interbank lending rates have shown fluctuations, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and an increase in capital market activities such as initial public offerings. Special Topic 4: Research on how market attention towards future initial public offerings affects three-month Hong Kong banks bank interbank lending rates. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting the banks' continued increase in preferential deposit interest rates to attract deposit funds. With some banks raising the interest rate ceiling set by the most favorable loan rates, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but due to the decrease in the most favorable loan rates in the market starting from November, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages slightly fell to around 2.5% by January 2020. Given the stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, stable Total reserves, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of Hong Kong dollars or the Hong Kong banking system or Hong Kong banks was observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact that a further worsening of the COVID-19 epidemic could bring in the situation where the external environment is unclear. Hong Kong possesses vast foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system; the Monetary Authority has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain the stability of the Hong Kong currency and financial system. During the review period, the market anticipated that China-US would reach a trade agreement, and offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates would strengthen; however, since the coronavirus pandemic epidemic broke out in late January 2020, it faced downward pressure. In 2019, offshore RMB generally exhibited a premium over onshore RMB; in January 2020, the discount temporarily widened, but the spread remained mild according to historical standards. The offshore RMB fund pool in Hong Kong slightly recovered after slightly fell during the previous review period. As of the end of January 2020, RMB customer deposits and certificate balances reached RMB 637.4 billion. Other RMB businesses in Hong Kong have also grown, with strong growth recorded in Hong Kong's RMB bank lending and RMB trade settlement businesses. The daily average transaction volume of the RMB real-time payment settlement system remained at a high level of 1133.9 billion RMB throughout the full year of 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of mainland capital accounts, increased allocation of RMB assets by international investors, and deepened regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilization, leading the market to anticipate a global economic recovery. However, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases since late January 2020 has dashed recovery hopes, deepened investors' concerns about a global economic recession, and triggered selling in global financial markets. In response to the economic impact, the main central banks and some governments have launched stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, the downside risks facing the global economic growth prospects have increased. In East Asia, the weakening of global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the prospects of the regional economies. The expected outbreak of coronavirus is anticipated to drag down regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism industry being particularly severely affected. On the other hand, the East Asia region continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. As for mainland China, due to weak domestic and external demand, economic growth continued to slow down in the second half of 2019. Looking ahead, although the first phase of the China-US trade agreement helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties, the downward pressure remains in the face of the outbreak of the coronavirus, continued economic rebalancing, and the slowdown of the global economy, and the monetary and fiscal policies adopted by the authorities to respond will provide some buffer. Under the influence of ongoing trade tensions and policy uncertainty, the manufacturing and investment sectors remained weak, and global economic growth remained sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth in the final quarter initially showed signs of stabilization (Figure 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier easing policies of the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of trade tensions following the signing of the initial phase of trade agreements between China-US. Figure 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index; however, since the end of January, the number of coronavirus infections has been continuously increasing, and the subsequent impact on the economy has caused market concern, leading to a sell-off in the global financial markets (Figure 2.2). Given that mainland China is a major global export destination and holds a significant position in the global supply chain, when the epidemic disrupts production activities in the mainland and drags down its economic growth, it will cause a significant spillover effect and may affect the global economy (Figure 2.3). Since the end of February, coronavirus infection cases have surged in regions outside mainland China, which may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and bring the risk of directly dragging down local economic activity. Figure 2.2 Morgan Stanley Capital International All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option Spread Adjustment Chart (Figure 2.3) In 2018, selected major advanced economies implemented measures to address the potential severe economic impact of the epidemic on the economy in mainland China, with some central banks (including the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) beginning to cut interest rates from early March, and some governments also introducing targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of the global financial situation, which may subsequently exacerbate the downward pressure on the global economy (Figure 2.4). (Figure 2.4) The Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index, in addition to the development of the epidemic, is also overshadowed by other downside risks and uncertainties affecting the global economy outlook. Especially regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased after China-US reached the first phase of the China-US trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may face numerous difficulties due to many thorny structural issues that still need to be resolved. On the European side, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to proceed smoothly, which will continue the uncertainty following the UK's withdrawal. Furthermore, oil prices have sharply declined since March, which will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, due to sluggish global demand, real economic activity remained weak in the second half of 2019. Exports from the East Asia region to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Figure 2.5). Although preliminary signs indicate that the downtrend cycle for local technology products is bottoming out and recovering, including that major local electronics companies have reported an improvement in their 2019 year-end earnings (6), whether exports of local technology products will see a substantive rebound remains to be observed. Figure 2.5 East Asia: Economic growth and trade uncertainty concerning the continued weakness in goods exports to major destinations also troubled investor sentiment, and the total fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies declined in 2019 (Figure 2.6), which may affect potential economic growth in the region in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered policy interest rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half of 2019, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy interest rate for the first time since 2015. Figure 2.6 East Asia: The outbreak of the coronavirus has led to concerns that economies in the region may face further pressure amid a slowdown in growth. Due to multiple economies in the region imposing entry and exit restrictions on mainland China, the tourism industry was hit hardest, particularly economies that rely heavily on tourists and tourism service exports from mainland China were more significantly affected by this epidemic (Figure 2.7). The ongoing and intensifying epidemic will also affect supply chains closely related to the region and mainland China. Figure 2.7 East Asia: In the short term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment regarding tourism exports and Chinese tourists. Referring to the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be temporary, but the actual situation will depend on the severity of the epidemic, the extent of its spread, and the effectiveness of the governments' actions to suppress the outbreak. At the same time, economies in East Asia also face multiple obstacles. Firstly, although market expectations suggest the company's earnings will deteriorate in the short term (Figure 2.8), the global accommodative monetary conditions encourage yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing asset prices higher without fundamental support. Therefore, the local stock market is more susceptible to the influence of changes in investor sentiment regarding investment. The expected returns of constituent stocks of the benchmark stock index, Figure 2.8, are secondary, and weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the region to repay debts. Although the decline in local interest rates may provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, it may also sow the hidden danger of further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as described in Special Topic 1, when more funds flow into the local financial markets with tracking indices, the risk of accumulated debt for private institutions may also be exacerbated, although this impact may be limited to corporations with more stable financial foundations and long-term borrowings. Third, regarding external factors, facing increasingly stringent trade policies from the United States, the risks faced by East Asian economies may also increase. Although progress has been made in the first phase of the China-US trade agreement recently, the fundamental issues between the two countries regarding trade still exist, and trade tensions between China-US continue. As the trade surplus with the United States continues to increase from multiple economies within the region (Figure 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek further sourcing channels outside of the China-centric supply chains to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging economies in Asia (excluding China) with the United States reached approximately $167 billion. If the trade surplus with the United States continues to expand, relevant Asian economies may become the next target of the trade war. For example, the United States governments imposed substantial tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the trade prospects in the region remain extremely unclear. Figure 2.9 shows that the trade surplus for goods in the United States over the past decade has significantly increased due to the intensification of global cross-border securities investment capital flows caused by the integration of international financial markets. A recent study indicates that up to seventy percent of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds. 8 Index-tracking funds not only include funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also include funds that actively manage based on investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors who would otherwise not have been attracted or accessed, these funds help to promote the development of the financial markets in emerging market economies through investment. Therefore, this type of fund enables emerging market economies to achieve investor base diversification for investment, which aids in long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really a free lunch in the world? For passive bond funds, the market is concerned that this type of fund investment may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bond issuers it invests in, thereby leading to high corporate leverage levels. Furthermore, some opinion suggests that the growth of index-tracking funds in recent years has exacerbated volatility in global securities investment capital flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors, even more vulnerable. This paper addresses these two propositions, evaluating the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability. Based on the weight of the bonds within the benchmark index in the index, the passive bond fund will allocate its investment capital to the relevant bonds. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, passive bond funds' mechanical investment decisions or the inclusion of bonds within the benchmark index lack the incentive to act from the perspective of fund investors' interests. 13 Worse still, from the perspective of financial stability, this behavior will foster excessive borrowing, bringing significant credit and debt servicing capacity risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies due to a sharp increase in leverage ratios following the global financial crisis (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1 estimates the weight of corporations in each emerging market economies within a mainstream index tracking emerging market economy corporate bonds as the investment by a passive bond fund in their bonds. We find that an increase in this type of investment will raise the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratio of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. Figure B1.2, the blue solid bar represents the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded investor base of the passive bond fund for long-term bond investment is also beneficial for the development of corporations in emerging market economies. We simultaneously found that the aforementioned effects have a significant impact only on firms in emerging market economies with more robust fundamentals (especially those with stronger debt-servicing capacity and lower leverage ratios) (green solid bars in Figure B1.2). Faced with higher financial distress costs, firms with high leverage or poor debt-servicing capacity do not appear to fall further into debt traps due to investment in passive bond fund investment. In summary, the above study indicates that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not significantly increase the debt-servicing capacity risk in the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Due to weakened private consumption, reduced investment spending, and poor export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered a recession for the first time since 2009. The economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the recent coronavirus pandemic has also brought considerable downside risk. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertain factors and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, U.S.-China trade relations, the economic performance of inland China, and the development of local social events. Given the various obstacles facing the economy, the unemployment rate may climb further in 2020. The expected pressure from domestic inflation will ease, but its outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. Hong Kong's economy significantly contracted in the second half of 2019. On an annual basis, real domestic gross value contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters, respectively (Table 3.A). Affected by the slowdown in the second half of the year's economy, the annual economic contraction was 1.2%, which is worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and is the first annual contraction recorded since the global financial crisis of 2009. Figure 3.1 Quarterly comparison of the real domestic gross value growth rate and the contribution of major expenditure items, with economic activity significantly slowing down in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, the real domestic gross value fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters, respectively, indicating that the economy has entered a recession. Locally, private consumption is the main factor dragging down the local Gross Domestic Product in the third quarter. Local social events severely impact consumption activities, consequently weakening the economy's prospects and damaging consumer confidence, so private consumption has significantly contracted starting in the third quarter. Due to increased uncertainty in the economy and a downturn in the business climate, total investment expenditure remained weak, dragging down the fourth quarter local Gross Domestic Product. 34 In the periphery, due to the intensification of the US-China trade friction, the slowdown in global economy growth, and the sharp decline in tourist arrivals to Hong Kong, Hong Kong's foreign trade performance continued to languish (Figure 3.2). 35 Under the impact of the sharp contraction in service exports, net exports dragged down the local Gross Domestic Product in the third quarter, but provided support for the local Gross Domestic Product growth in the fourth quarter, partially reflecting an improvement in the trade balance of goods. Figure 3.2 In view of the significant obstacles facing the economy, the government launched multiple measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on citizens, ensure employment, and support businesses, particularly by assisting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and industries severely impacted, such as retail, food services, transportation, and tourism. 36 To provide banks with greater room to increase support for the locally economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Monetary Authority announced on October 14 that the banks' countercyclical buffer ratio would be lowered from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby allowing banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 to 300 billion to corporations, including SMEs. The economy in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the pandemic recently has also brought significant downside risk. Because some industries have not yet recovered after the damage caused by social events, the pandemic will bring a dual blow to these industries. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 fiscal budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (especially SMEs), including the distribution of a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee for businesses under the "SMEs Financing Guarantee Scheme." On March 16, 2020, the Monetary Authority further lowered the countercyclical buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will allow banks greater room to intensify support for the locally economy, especially for industries and individuals who are under greater short-term pressure due to the pandemic. Analyzing by components of the local Gross Domestic Product, due to fragile consumption and business confidence, private consumption and investment may remain weak. Although government consumption will support the economy's growth, with the completion of some major infrastructure projects, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued. Regarding external factors, the first phase of the China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the locally economy in the short term. However, the weakness in global economy growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's foreign trade performance. Especially the outbreak of the coronavirus may lead to disruptions in the supply chain within the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activity (such as the tourism sector), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts that the real local Gross Domestic Product will grow between -1.5% and 0.5% in 2020, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. These weak economy's prospects are affected by the numerous uncertain factors and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and the beginning of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and further climbed to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among them, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors rose to a ten-year high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe impact of social events. As the economy's momentum weakened, the overall number of employed persons fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment numbers mainly comes from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in response to the aforementioned weak economy's prospects, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is likely to rise further. Special Topic 3 will explore in greater detail the recent developments and short-term prospects of the labor market. Figure 3.3 The domestic inflation pressure continued to accumulate until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices on the labor market Locally. Subsequent economic activity weakened, and the inflationary impetus also gradually eased. Compared year-on-year, the Consumer Price Index increased by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the growth rate slightly slowed to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The basic inflation rate, calculated on a three-month to annual rate reflecting the inflationary impetus, softened from the high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in the inflationary impetus is due to a reduction in price pressure on the components of the consumer price index. In terms of trade goods, the rise in fresh pork prices has caused basic food inflation to remain noticeable, although price pressure on consumer goods such as clothing and durable goods remains mild. In terms of services, as the growth of rental components in the consumer price index for private residential housing has slowed down, the growth of the rental component of the consumer price index also shows a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressure has slightly increased, but has remained at a moderate level in the recent few quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 reflects different indicators of consumer price inflation, Figure 3.5 shows the composite consumer price index, rent items, and market rent, Figure 3.6 shows unit labor costs, and the domestic inflation pressure is expected to ease in the short term. Locally, the weak economy situation and the widening output gap will continue to constitute downside pressure on local inflation. As private residential housing rents continue to slow down, housing rent items in inflation should be further eased. On the periphery, due to weak global economy growth and soft energy prices, import inflation is expected to remain moderate. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate for 2020 will be between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts the basic inflation rate to be 2.5% and the overall inflation rate to be 1.7%. This inflation outlook is affected by risks from both the upside and the downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the severity of the economy's deterioration is worse than expected (for example, due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic), it may further suppress inflation. On the other hand, if the supply of fresh pork becomes more constrained, it will bring upside pressure to inflation. Although Hong Kong's economy has clearly slowed, the unemployment rate remained at a low of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. As social events continued, the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus pandemic, the labor market will face greater resistance in 2020. In this context, this study analyzes the recent development and short-term outlook of the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market was relatively stable in the first three quarters of 2019 (with almost no change in the unemployment rate) and what implications this has for future development. This paper also examines some risk factors that may lead to a sharp increase in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator because some adjustments to labor demand require costs. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags the annual growth rate of the real domestic gross value by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagged nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at approximately 2.9% when real economic activity sharply deteriorated in the third quarter of the economy. Figure B3.1: Regarding the real local Gross Domestic Product growth rate and the unemployment rate, although the tense China-US trade situation and local social events have dealt a heavy blow to employment in the trade, retail, and tourism-related industries, some key industries can still support the overall labor market. Specifically, the employment numbers in the finance, business, public administration, social, and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment numbers in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's finance system remains stable, and finance activities in the development of fintech and new share issuance are also very active. These factors may support the employment market in the finance and business services industry. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the public administration, social, and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, to the economy cycle appears to be relatively low. Related coefficient analysis shows that although the employment numbers of many industries are highly correlated with the real domestic gross value, the response of public administration, social, and personal services sectors to the economy cycle is relatively neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows down, the employment numbers in these industries may not be significantly affected by the cycle. Figure B3.2 shows the change in employment numbers across various industries in 2019, with the labor force participation rate decreasing from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer for the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bar) exerts downside pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment numbers in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped to suppress the unemployment rate. However, the economy is significantly contracting in the second half of the year, and the decrease in employment numbers puts upside pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment numbers decreased during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure of the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019 economy. Figure B3.3 factors causing changes in the unemployment rate and some changes in the labor market structure are also worth noting. Especially the increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees or the ability to retain employees for the company. In fact, the proportion of self-employed individuals and underemployed individuals of the total employment numbers has decreased to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, but the number of voluntary part-time employees continues to rise, becoming the second-largest group of the total working population (approximately 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, the company can retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to approximately 44 hours currently, partly reflecting a greater number of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with the upward momentum further strengthening in December, which has kept the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate within the exchange guarantee range for the past few months. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar is partly due to stock-related demand, and partly due to the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar caused by liquidity tightening near the end of the year. Overall, the operation of the Hong Kong foreign exchange and currency market continues smoothly and orderly. Although the COVID-19 pandemic may cause increased volatility in capital flows due to uncertain external environments, Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding the pressure of capital outflows without affecting the financial stability of Hong Kong. Supported by increased demand for the Hong Kong dollar related to stocks (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Figure 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar was further strengthened, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained in the bullish range of the exchange guarantee. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened, partly due to the robust activity in initial public offerings, and partly due to the unwinding of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar caused by liquidity tightening near the end of the year. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, the liquidity situation has eased, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has slightly weakened, closing at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued smoothly and orderly during the review period. As the strong or weak exchange rate guarantees were not triggered during the review period, the total balance remained unchanged, approximately 54 billion Hong Kong dollar (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1, Figure 4.2, and the nominal effective exchange rate index for the total balance of foreign exchange fund instruments and bonds in Hong Kong dollar generally followed the movement of the US dollar, with a slight increase during the review period (Figure 4.3). Due to the small difference in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the impact on the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar is limited, and the trend of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index generally follows the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3 The nominal and real effective exchange rates must distinguish between two distinct yet interrelated concepts of capital flows when measuring the capital flows of Hong Kong: (1) Hong Kong dollar capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. Hong Kong dollar capital flows focus on the monetary aspect of capital flows, which aids in assessing monetary stability, especially under the linked exchange rate system. On the other hand, cross-border capital flows focus on the movement of funds between regions through the Hong Kong banking system, which aids in assessing the stability of the overall Hong Kong financial system. Two concepts of capital flows require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring Hong Kong dollar capital flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the total balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, the demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decrease, leading to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the linked exchange rate system, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the floor exchange rate of 7.85 Hong Kong dollars to 1 US dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will be prepared at any time to purchase Hong Kong dollars at the request of banks, and the total balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the total balance has remained largely unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been in the strong position within the exchange guarantee in recent months, therefore, no significant capital flows out of the Hong Kong dollar have been observed during the period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, the total amount of bank deposits in Hong Kong is a useful indicator. When a large amount of funds flows out of the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, the total deposit amount grew at a steady pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflows. The operation of the Hong Kong foreign exchange and currency market continues smoothly and orderly, which indicates that the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Hong Kong monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks brought by the COVID-19 pandemic. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system; the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain the financial stability of the Hong Kong currency and finance. Despite the unclear external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The Hong Kong dollar monetary base remains substantial, rising by 4.0% since the end of June to HK$16.894 trillion at the end of January 2020 (Figure 4.4). As the exchange rate guarantees were not triggered during this period, therefore the total balance remained largely unchanged, approximately 54 billion Hong Kong dollar. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds, debt certificates, as well as circulating banknotes and coins issued by the government, are steadily rising. The components of the monetary base in Figure 4.4 generally remained stable during the review period, with a broad measure of Hong Kong dollar money supply. The Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and subsequently increased by 0.2% over the seven months up to the end of June 2019. Over the seven months since the end of June, the Hong Kong dollar deposits (the main component of Hong Kong dollar M3) have remained largely unchanged (Figure 4.6). In Hong Kong dollar deposits, fixed-term deposits continue to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in Hong Kong dollar deposit interest rates. Due to fluctuations in monthly currency statistics, which can be affected by various short-term factors (such as seasonality, public offering-related capital demands, and business and investment activities), statistical figures should be interpreted with caution. Although the monetary environment remains relatively loose, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank lending rates among peers experienced fluctuations, reflecting seasonality in liquidity demand, as well as increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the increased activity of initial public offerings in the Hong Kong stock market. Overnight interbank lending rates among Hong Kong banks experienced greater volatility in late October and mid-November (Figure 4.8). During the review period, interbank rates among other short-term Hong Kong banks generally rose. The large new share listing subscription event puts significant pressure on overnight call rates, and a specialized analysis shows that market attention towards future initial public offerings will also affect three-month Hong Kong banks' interbank call rates. This situation will occur if market participants anticipate the future offering date for the listing of large new shares in advance and prepare mid-term funds for early deployment. Figure 4.8 shows that the interbank lending rates in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar, as well as the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, follow the downward shift of the US dollar yield curve. Figure 4.9 The yield on government bonds, the composite interest rate, and the average loan interest rate for new mortgages at the retail level, reflecting the composite interest rate of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This rise mainly reflects banks continuing to increase preferential deposit interest rates to attract deposit funds, and consequently, the Hong Kong dollar weighted deposit interest rate has risen. Regarding mortgage loans, for mortgage loans based on the interbank lending rates of Hong Kong banks, major banks raised the upper limit of the interest rate determined by the most favorable loan rate, so the average loan interest rate for new mortgages in October rose to around 2.63%. The most favorable loan rate in the market has decreased since November, with the average mortgage loans rate slightly falling to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the constantly evolving risks that the COVID-19 pandemic poses to the US economic activity, and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on March 3 (US time) and March 15 (US time). Although interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks will follow the fluctuations in US dollar interest rates in the long run, short-term interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks may be affected by local factors influencing Hong Kong dollar demand, such as new share listings in Hong Kong. The total balance of the banking system has decreased since April 2018, and the sensitivity of Hong Kong banks' interbank lending rates to changes in the supply and demand for Hong Kong dollar funds may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current total balance of 54 billion Hong Kong dollar is insufficient to meet the demand for interbank payment settlements. In fact, the banking industry in Hong Kong has always operated in an orderly manner. If liquidity is short-term tight, banks can use the liquidity arrangements provided to banks by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. Given the potential escalation of the US-China trade conflict, offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates significantly weakened in late August and September 2019; the offshore RMB against the US dollar fell to a ten-year low of 7.19 on September 2 (Figure 4.10). Entering October, with expectations in the market of the resumption of US-China trade negotiations, the trend of RMB depreciation reversed, and offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter, and after the signing of the first phase of the trade agreement between China and the US, it once surpassed the 6.9 level in January 2020. However, since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic at the end of January, offshore and onshore RMB have once again faced pressure to weaken. The offshore RMB generally presented a discount against the onshore RMB from May to August, and in 2019, it generally presented a premium in the later period. At the end of January 2020, the discount temporarily widened, but the spread between the two still remains moderate according to historical standards. Figure 4.10, despite fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate, the liquidity situation in the offshore RMB banking industry market has remained largely stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore RMB Hong Kong banks interbank lending rates continued to hover between 3-4% (Figure 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB interbank lending rates in Hong Kong banks experienced a temporary fluctuation in late August and late November due to adjustments in A-shares by Morgan Stanley International Capital (MSCI), and near the Lunar New Year holiday at the end of January 2020.

Due to increasing uncertainties in the global and Hong Kong economic environment, the profitability of Hong Kong retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity situation of the Hong Kong banking industry remains strong and stable when measured by international standards. By historical standards, the asset quality remains at a healthy level. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still grew faster than deposits during the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio calculated in all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio have both increased. However, given that the overall reserves of the banking system are at a stable level and deposits are largely stable, the liquidity situation of the banking industry remains sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking industry will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertain factors such as the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continuous increase in corporate leverage and personal debt burden, the bank should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of its loan portfolio under conditions where these risk factors may be exacerbated. Although the net interest margin of the retail bank narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), the net interest income of the retail bank continued to grow moderately during the review period. However, loan loss provisions and operating expenses for the retail bank have both increased, leading to a slight decrease in profitability. Looking ahead, various downside risk factors in the external and local environments will continue to cast a shadow over the bank's profitability prospects. Relevant factors include the uncertainty arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of US-China trade relations, and the exacerbation of geopolitical tensions. The exacerbation of these risk factors will undermine the already weakened global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given that major central banks are widely adopting accommodative monetary policies, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, which could put pressure on the net interest margin of banks in the future. At the local level, local social events that began in mid-2019 continue to undermine commercial investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of a weakening economic environment, if the situation continues or further deteriorates in the future, it will lead to a deterioration in credit demand prospects and the asset quality of the bank. In terms of overall market development, following the issuance of eight virtual bank licenses by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking industry has begun to launch virtual bank services. Due to the possibility that these new market participants may attract new customers to increase their market share by launching more convenient products and more attractive deposit interest rates, this may exert upward pressure on the financing costs of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may still be mild due to the limited current business scale of virtual banks, their long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the application of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Special Topic 5 indicate that the degree to which banks in Hong Kong adopt financial technology has a statistical correlation with improvements in cost-effectiveness and increases in profitability. The capital of the Hong Kong banking industry remains sound and far exceeds the minimum international standards.
