The introduction of the novel coronavirus vaccine brings hope for an economic restart and boosts global growth prospects. Coupled with continuous fiscal and monetary easing policies, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains shrouded by uncertainties, with the pace of recovery varying across different economies. In the medium term, the decoupling of the financial markets from the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-term damage inflicted on the economy by the pandemic will be challenges facing decision-makers in the future. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and monetary markets continue to operate smoothly and orderly. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate is near the forward exchange guarantee level, mainly driven by stock-related demand. During the review period, the total deposit amount increased, with no indication of significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong banking system. Some reflect that the recurrent pandemic has led to weakened economic activity and reduced credit demand, with the total loan amount in the banking sector slightly decreasing in the second half of the year, although it still recorded a slight increase when measured for the full year of 2020. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained relatively stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding the pace of economic recovery and ongoing geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. Especially the pandemic will weaken the repayment capacity of enterprises and households, and the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies resumed in various regions, but as the number of novel coronavirus infections increased from the fourth quarter, global growth slowed again. Nevertheless, with the breakthrough in vaccine research at the end of 2020, market expectations are that the pandemic will ultimately end, benefiting the global economy's return to normalcy and accelerated growth. In addition to the continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, global financial markets reached a new high in early 2021, despite signs of decoupling from the real economy beginning to emerge. In this context, uncertainties will continue to overshadow the global economy outlook. The widespread distribution of vaccines is still to be observed. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier easing policies could lead to inflation higher than expected, subsequently requiring the central bank to reduce monetary easing in advance, ending the financial markets' expectation of "longer-term low-interest" monetary policy. In the long term, decision-makers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures, and address numerous economic legacy issues triggered by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic trauma. In the Asia-Pacific region, the growth in domestic Gross Domestic Product in the second half of 2020 improved, supported by the rebound in export demand. With the increase in risk appetite, securities investment funds in the region are flowing back in, and yield-seeking activities are reappearing. Despite the aforementioned positive developments, the Asia-Pacific region still needs to face the ongoing uncertainties brought by the pandemic. Firstly, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, economies with lower levels of development within the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service industries. Secondly, the supply, coverage, or efficacy of vaccines may be variable, coupled with a weakening of the local government fiscal situation, which could lead to a deterioration in market sentiment and trigger a reversal of capital flows. As for mainland China, with consumption activities gradually recovering to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking at the full year 2020, the mainland economies grew by 2.3%, being the only economies to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic prospects still largely depend on the development of the pandemic and the changes in Sino-US relations. The latest consensus forecast indicates that the mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi experienced several months of depreciation at the beginning of 2020, and subsequently strengthened in the remaining time of the year as the economic recovery accelerated, the dollar weakened, and strong capital flows entered the mainland bond market. Detailed research shows that during the outbreak of the novel coronavirus, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more significant role in driving the fluctuations of the renminbi (see Study 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real local gross domestic product remained far below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in local demand and further expansion of goods exports, real local gross domestic product, adjusted for seasonality, began to recover in the third quarter, ending the previous five consecutive quarters of contraction. The annual contraction rate of the real local gross domestic product narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to approximately 3% in the second half. However, for the full year 2020, the real local gross domestic product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and this is the first time in history that there has been a consecutive two-year decline after a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest data on gross domestic product in different industries shows that the contraction in the consumption and tourism-related sectors was worse under the pandemic than in the overall economy. The government launched two rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of epidemic prevention and control funds in the second half of 2020 to help industries and residents affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's epidemic prevention and control capacity. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 fiscal budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 e-consumption voucher and a 100% guaranteed personal preferential loan for the unemployed. The Monetary Authority also announced in March 2021 that the "pre-approval for interest-only repayment without principal repayment" scheme would be extended until October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme within the banking sector. It is anticipated that these extension measures will help alleviate some of the working capital difficulties faced by enterprise clients. The novel coronavirus vaccines are expected to restore normal economic activity, with local economies projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (full year total), but the pace and strength of the economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollouts. Given the time required for widespread vaccines, local economies still faced significant challenges in the early part of 2021. Regarding external factors, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which can provide support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccines programs. The government forecasts that the real local gross domestic product will grow between 3.5–5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. The labor market situation further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and the beginning of 2021. The unemployment rate further climbed to a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a high level since the pandemic. In response to the continuously deteriorating labor market situation, the government launched the "Job Retention" scheme under the second round of epidemic prevention and control funds, providing employers with temporary wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to assist them in retaining employees. After the "Job Security" plan concluded, the government launched other targeted measures (such as a one-off subsidy) under the third round and the fourth round of epidemic prevention and control funds to further support industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, due to the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Special Topic 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of the Hong Kong tourism industry on the local labor market. Local inflation pressure weakened over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The core consumer price inflation rate significantly decreased year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third quarter of 2020 and the fourth quarter, and further fell to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February of 2021. The basic inflation rate, calculated as an annualized rate over three months reflecting the drivers of inflation, has remained at a low level in recent months, despite slight fluctuations. Due to ongoing challenges in both global and local economies, Hong Kong inflation pressure may remain slight in the short term, particularly as the slowdown in the growth of previously signed private residential rental increases will continue to curb local inflation, and the current economic conditions suggest this trend will persist. The market consensus forecast for the overall inflation rate in 2021 is at a moderate level of 1.4%, whereas The government forecasts the core and headline inflation rates for 2021 to be 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The Hong Kong dollar is near the forward exchange guarantee level, primarily driven by capital flows related to stock demands, including new share fundraising activities from Changwang, as well as southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong channels. The fundraising activities during the first two months of 2021 remained active, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain strong. During the review period, the strong party's exchange guarantee was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with funds flowing into the Hong Kong dollar amounting to HK$263.3 billion. The strong party's exchange guarantee was triggered a total of 85 times during the full year 2020, accumulating an inflow of 383.5 billion Hong Kong dollar. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continue smoothly and orderly. From a geographical perspective, during the review period, the total deposit amount increased, which shows no indication of significant capital flows out of the Hong Kong banking system. Despite uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the Sino-US relationship remaining tense, which may exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows, Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system, and is therefore capable of withstanding fluctuations in capital flows. With the triggering of the strong party's exchange guarantee leading to an increase in total reserves, interbank lending rates in Hong Kong dollar banks' peer group generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate reflecting the average cost of retail bank Hong Kong dollar funds further decreased from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021; due to the reduction in funding costs, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages also decreased from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the preferential lending rates for major retail banks will remain unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. With the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) has appreciated against the dollar since late May 2020. During most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate had a premium compared to the onshore renminbi exchange rate, with the average premium in the fourth quarter approximately 100 points, which is still considered mild according to historical standards. The offshore renminbi liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the total balance of renminbi customer deposits and time deposits reaching RMB 826.3 billion as of the end of January of 2021. As for other renminbi business, Hong Kong renminbi bank loans decreased, while renminbi trade settlements increased, and the daily average transaction volume of the renminbi real-time payment settlement system remained at a high of 1191.5 billion renminbi throughout the full year 2020. Hong Kong possesses efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous cross-border capital flows channels to the mainland. With the continued opening of mainland capital accounts, increasing demand for renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Greater Bay Area initiatives, the offshore renminbi business in Hong Kong is expected to benefit. Under the support of the global stock market rise and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by mainland investors through the Stock Connect, the Hong Kong stock market experienced a rebound after a significant adjustment at the beginning of the review period. The rise in the global stock market is due to the unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies. The market is optimistic about the positive progress in vaccine research, believing this may help accelerate the recovery of economic activity. And the uncertainties in global geopolitics have decreased. Against the aforementioned background, the Hang Seng Index recovered after the sharp decline in 2020, increased by 15.1% during the review period, and briefly broke through the 31,000-point level in mid-February 2021, setting a 32-month high. Under stable issuance volume support, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following a large net outflow of funds in the first half of 2020, as the government in various countries launched unprecedented economic stimulus measures, the market confidence rapidly recovered, and bond funds flowing into the local market experienced a rebound. Although bond yields have rebounded moderately during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remain near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine research, the market expects the novel coronavirus pandemic to finally be concluded, allowing the global economy to accelerate its growth. Coupled with the expectation of "longer-term low interest rates" in global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the post-pandemic rebound at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached a new high in early 2021. However, the fervent expectations of the financial markets are out of sync with the still challenging macroeconomic environment; if the pace of economic recovery is not as ideal, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for example, due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could experience volatility. Looking to the future, the decision-making authorities will face the challenge of when to withdraw policy support, and how to address numerous issues left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic trauma. The continued uncertainty of the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in the East Asian region, and emerging market economies with slower development within the area may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. If the progress of the vaccination program is impeded, it may reverse the current optimistic sentiment, leading to decreased capital inflow and instability in the financial markets. As for inland China, with consumption activities gradually recovering to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the prospects for economic growth remain uncertain, largely depending on the development of the pandemic and changes in the Sino-US tensions. Therefore, the government has announced its continued supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the economic reopening, most major economies recorded real Gross Domestic Product growth that was better than expected in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of novel coronavirus infections has risen again, prompting local governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and the global growth momentum has weakened once more. At the end of 2020, a more transmissible variant of the virus emerged, which subsequently spread worldwide, making the situation more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine research and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020, market expectations are that the pandemic will ultimately be concluded, and the global economy will return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economy recovery comes from sustained policy stimulus measures, including the monetary policy of major central banks promising "longer-term low interest rates" amid weakening inflation, and the continuous fiscal easing measures by major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus package passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from the forecast made in October 2020 (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1 The real Gross Domestic Product growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020, in this context, strengthened market optimism, typically benefiting from the rise in stock prices of cyclical industries due to the economic recovery, driving global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Figure 2.2). The 12-month estimated price-to-earnings ratio for major stock indices in Figure 2.2; however, while the financial markets are performing strongly, the macroeconomic environment remains challenging, and the divergence between the two may lead to volatility in asset markets under multiple risks. First, the outlook for controlling the pandemic depends on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which is yet to be observed. As of March 2021, the global overall vaccination rate remained low (Figure 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) promote a fairer distribution of vaccines, the issue of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies will likely be more severe due to limited vaccine supply. If the pandemic control is not as ideal, various regions may need to continue social distancing and other restrictions, thereby undermining the prospects for global recovery. Figure 2.3 shows the proportion of the population in selected economies who have received at least one dose of vaccines (as of March 15, 2021); secondly, the rebound in the financial markets is based on continuous monetary and fiscal policy support, especially "longer-term low interest rates" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that the withdrawal of support measures will be faster than expected. For example, under the multiple effects of supply bottlenecks, strong currency and liquidity growth, and proactive fiscal easing policies, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have risen (Figure 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, the central bank may need to reduce the scale of monetary easing policy, and inflation data exceeding expectations may also lead to greater volatility in the financial markets. The third benchmark for 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates for the United States and the Eurozone, Figure 2.4, indicates significant uncertainty in future Sino-US relations. The US-China "decoupling" wave, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the pandemic broke out. Given the increasingly hardened stance of the Republican and Democratic parties in the United States toward inland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden government. Should the US-China situation unexpectedly escalate, it may trigger turmoil in the financial markets in the future. Looking to the future, decision-makers will need to face the issue of whether and when to withdraw the epidemic prevention support measures. Although prematurely withdrawing related measures could jeopardize economic recovery, causing a "cliff effect," in the long run, the costs of these measures are high, including the fiscal burden and the delay in the necessary reallocation of post-epidemic resources, such as allowing "zombie enterprises" whose business models are no longer viable to continue receiving government support. Furthermore, decision-makers must also address the numerous issues left by the pandemic. Firstly, due to declining corporate revenue and increased government expenditure, the global debt level rose significantly in 2020 (Figure 2.5). Although the issues arising from the rapid increase in debt due to the current extremely low global interest rates may not be imminent, the continued accumulation of debt by both public and private sectors may cause market concern regarding fiscal sustainability and financial stability. (Figure 2.5) The proportion of global debt to gross domestic product is another outstanding issue, and the other issue involves the long-term economic losses or lasting trauma that the pandemic may cause. For example, high uncertainty may lead to a reduction in investment by the corporate, and workers long troubled by unemployment may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a large waste of human resources. In East Asia, real gross domestic product recovered in the second half of the year after a sharp decline in the second quarter of 2020 (Figure 2.6). The main driver of the economic recovery comes from the rebound in exports, with the demand for exports of electronic and technology equipment being the most eager. Meanwhile, the service industry most severely hit (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face interaction with customers) continues to be in difficulty. (Figure 2.6) East Asia: Despite uncertainties in the economic recovery, real gross domestic product growth in 2020 saw securities investment funds re-enter. Since the second half of last year, due to improved market sentiment and higher yields on bonds compared to developed economies, the region has attracted more capital inflow for bonds (Figure 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the launch of vaccine production plans, stock funds also accelerated inflow to the East Asian region in the last quarter of 2020. The local currency also appreciated in response to the capital inflow from securities, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Yuan Index to rebound by approximately 10% from its low in March of last year. Figure 2.7 East Asia: Securities investment funds in the East Asian region continue to face persistent uncertainties due to the pandemic. Firstly, although the introduction of vaccines brings hope to the severely affected service industry and economic in the region, competition for early-batch vaccines worldwide has increased procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacity. Therefore, economic entities with slower development within the region may achieve herd immunity more slowly than developed economies, and uneven vaccination rates between economic entities may extend lockdown periods and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Secondly, since investor optimism is largely driven by the introduction of vaccines, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls significantly short of expectations, the current capital inflow and the rebound in financial asset prices may cease. A sharp decrease in capital inflow will trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the successful control of the novel coronavirus and the gradual recovery of consumption, the domestic economic recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. Concurrently, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical equipment and high-technology products), exports also maintained growth (Figure 2.8). Looking at 2020, despite the economic encountering unprecedented shock under the novel coronavirus pandemic, China's domestic gross domestic product still recorded a growth of 2.3%. The latest consensus forecast predicts that China's domestic economic will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the main driver of economic growth. Although industrial production activities in China's mainland have normalized, the service industry is still partially disrupted as the pandemic reappears in several northern provinces. Although the real Gross Domestic Product remains significantly lower than pre-pandemic levels, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 with the recovery in local demand and further expansion of goods exports. Anticipating that the vaccination against the novel coronavirus will allow economic activities to return to normal, Hong Kong's economy is expected to recover growth in 2021 after recording the most severe contraction since 2020. However, the pace and strength of economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertain factors, such as the development of the epidemic, the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccine inoculation, the Hong Kong economy still faced significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure in the short term, and domestic inflation pressure remains slight. The Hong Kong economy showed improvement in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained far below pre-epidemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real Gross Domestic Product narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the full year of 2020, the real Gross Domestic Product fell by 6.1%, the largest decline since record time, and this is the first time in history that there has been a consecutive two-year decline following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data from various industries also shows that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors has declined year-on-year in recent quarters, with the contraction in the consumption and tourism-related industries being more severe than the overall economy. Compared on a quarterly basis, real Gross Domestic Product began to recover starting from the third quarter of 2020, ending a five-quarter decline (Table 3.A and Figure 3.1). Local private consumption recovered to positive growth in the third quarter and fourth quarter; however, under the local third and fourth waves of the epidemic, as the authorities reimposed social distancing measures, consumer confidence remained weak. With the business climate temporarily recovering, overall investment expenditure also increased in the second half of the year. Partially benefiting from the strengthening export performance (especially exports to mainland China), Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). Due to the stagnation of the global tourism industry, service trade remains weak. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged down the GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower pace of goods exports compared to imports. Figure 3.1 real Gross Domestic Product growth rate and contribution of major expenditure items Figure 3.2 real trade balance and government measures to respond to the ongoing epidemic, the government re-launched two rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of epidemic prevention and control funds totaling HK$30.4 billion from September to December 2020 to assist affected industries and residents and to enhance Hong Kong's epidemic prevention and control capacity. The government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 fiscal budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-time HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100% guaranteed personal preferential loan for the unemployed. The Monetary Authority also announced in March 2021 that the "pre-approval for interest-only repayment without principal repayment" scheme would be extended until October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme for the industries. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate some of the working capital difficulties faced by corporate clients. The novel coronavirus vaccine is expected to restore normal economic activity, with projections that the Hong Kong economy will resume positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), but the pace and strength of the economic recovery are influenced by numerous uncertain factors, including the development of the epidemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given the time required for widespread vaccine inoculation, the local economy still faced significant challenges in early 2021. Regarding external factors, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which can provide support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccine programs, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism industry. The government forecasts that the real Gross Domestic Product for the full year 2021 will grow between 3.5–5.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. The labor market situation further deteriorated in the second half of 2020 and the beginning of 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate further climbed to 7.2% in February 2021, a high level in 17 years (Figure 3.3). The unemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a high level after the epidemic. After the total number of employed persons fell to a low point and stabilized (Figure 3.3), government figures show that the number of job vacancies continues to decline. The nominal average wage index for employed persons reflecting labor income slowed to a growth rate of 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the continuously deteriorating labor market situation, the government launched the "Job Security" scheme under the second round of epidemic prevention and control funds, providing employers with temporary wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to assist them in retaining employees. After the "Job Security" program concluded, the government launched other targeted measures (such as a one-off subsidy) under the epidemic prevention and control funds in the third round and the fourth round to further support industries severely affected by the epidemic. In the short term, due to the weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Special Topic 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of the inbound tourism industry on the local labor market. Figure 3.3 labor market situation and Figure 3.4 reflect different indicators of consumption price inflation; domestic inflation pressure weakened over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The basic consumption price inflation rate significantly decreased year-on-year to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third quarter of 2020 and the fourth quarter of 2020, and further fell to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February of 2021, respectively (Figure 3.4). The core inflation rate, calculated as an annualized rate over three months reflecting inflationary momentum, has remained at a low level, although with slight fluctuations, in recent months. Specifically, the price pressure on basic food has eased, and dining out expenses have clearly decreased, reflecting more restaurants offering takeout promotions during periods when dine-in service is restricted. Price pressure on other trade goods (such as durable goods) remains mild. In terms of services, with the stabilization of private residential rents, the rental component of the consumer consumption price index remains weak (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressure has eased in the recent quarters (Figure 3.6). Particularly affected by the slowdown in the growth of private residential rents previously signed, local inflation will continue to be contained. Market consensus forecasts that the overall inflation rate for 2021 will be at a mild level of 1.4%, while the government forecasts the core inflation rate for 2021 to be 1% and the overall inflation rate to be 1.6%. With the rampant epidemic of the novel coronavirus, the inbound tourism industry has rapidly entered a recession, and the market is concerned that this crisis will have a traumatic effect on the future labor market recovery. Therefore, this special empirical analysis examines the impact of the boom in the inbound tourism industry on the Hong Kong labor market, and explores the potential effects of the current downturn in the tourism industry. Since 2000, the inbound tourism industry has experienced significant ups and downs (Figure B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitors to Hong Kong decreased during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic in 2003. Since the "Personal Travel" plan (free travel) was launched in July of the same year, the number of tourists began to surge. Under the original free travel scheme, mainland residents can apply individually for visits to Hong Kong once or twice a year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The free travel scheme has been expanded since April 2009, allowing eligible residents holding Shenzhen residency to apply for a one-year multiple-entry "Personal Travel" visa (multiple entries) to Hong Kong. From now on, the number of domestic tourists has significantly increased. Driven by the development of new cross-border infrastructure in mainland China, the number of visitors to Hong Kong reached a new historical high from the end of 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social events caused visitor numbers to be halved in the second half of 2019, and under the novel coronavirus epidemic, the inbound tourism industry has been stagnant since the end of January 2020. (Figure B2.1) passenger numbers and related policies, we will explore the impact of the inbound tourism industry on local employment and income using the prosperity of tourism brought by the free travel scheme for visitors to Hong Kong. We believe that the free travel scheme launched in 2003 is similar to a random economic shock, because it is almost exogenously timed, and residents of Hong Kong could not have predicted its launch. Our primary analytical data comes from population data in the Hong Kong census or mid-term population statistics. Specifically, we use a 5% sample from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 censuses or mid-term population statistics. Furthermore, we also define the tourism-related industries as the food, retail, hotel, and transportation industries. First, we adopt the "difference-in-differences" as the analytical framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes between young workers (20-40 years old) in the "treatment group" and older workers (41-65 years old) in the "comparison group" before and after the implementation of the free travel scheme. We will place the younger group in the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can make significant changes to their employment decisions more flexibly in response to the exogenously growing inbound tourism industry of visitors to Hong Kong. Due to the impact of the boom in the tourism industry brought about by the free travel scheme on the labor market being subject to change over time, we also adopt the "event study" method to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical research results indicate that compared to older groups, young workers (especially women and those with only a high school education) are more likely to enter industries related to tourism after the implementation of the free travel scheme. Among these, the free travel scheme has a particularly significant and sustained impact on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries, remaining at a level close to five percentage points (compared to the average difference in employment probability for older groups) since 2006 (Figure B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare the revenue from tourism-related industries (treatment group) with non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimated results show that after the implementation of the free travel scheme, the income growth of workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Furthermore, the income growth rate for women workers and low-educated workers employed in tourism-related industries is higher and shows an upward trend compared to counterparts in other industries (3-20 percentage points) (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2 shows the impact of the free travel scheme on women's employment, and Figure B2.3 shows the impact of the free travel scheme on the income of women and low-skilled workers. The above results are generally consistent with international experience, revealing that the tourism industry is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women, and workers with lower educational attainment. Regarding the situation in Hong Kong, our research findings are consistent with previous analyses, indicating that the strong growth in the inbound tourism industry has increased the market's demand for lower-skilled labor, thereby improving the stability of the labor market for visitors to Hong Kong in the lower-skilled segment. As the inbound tourism industry for visitors to Hong Kong falls to a trough, these labor groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continues to remain close to the strength-based exchange guarantee level, and the strength-based exchange guarantee was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar is mainly driven by capital demand related to stocks, including new share issuance activities from Changwang, as well as southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong channels. With total reserves increasing to over 450 billion Hong Kong dollar, interbank lending rates in Hong Kong have all fallen. Despite uncertain factors related to the development of the novel coronavirus epidemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions between China and the United States, capital flow volatility may be exacerbated; however, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a stable banking system, enabling it to withstand the pressure from capital flow fluctuations. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate is close to the strength-based exchange guarantee level, mainly driven by capital demand related to stocks, including new share issuance activities from Changwang, as well as southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong channels (Figure 4.1). Although some of the funds raised from the initial public offering have been withdrawn, due to the improving sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market and rising funding demand as market expectations approached the end of the year, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate fluctuated narrowly between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December. With the fundraising activities remaining active during the first two months of 2021 (Figure 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar closed at 7.7568 on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continue smoothly and orderly. During the review period, the strength-based exchange guarantee was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in total reserves, reflecting a large inflow of Hong Kong dollar. The strength-based exchange guarantee was triggered 47 times from September 2020 to October. Based on the design of the linked exchange rate system, the People's Bank of China jointly sold 263.3 billion Hong Kong dollar, increasing the total reserves from 193.1 billion Hong Kong dollar at the end of August to 457.5 billion Hong Kong dollar at the end of February (Figure 4.3). The strength-based exchange guarantee was triggered a total of 85 times in 2020, with a cumulative inflow of 383.5 billion Hong Kong dollar. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicates no signs of significant capital outflow from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of any unusual capital flows. Figure 4.1, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, Figure 4.2, and Figure 4.3 of the stock funds raised by the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX), total reserves, foreign exchange fund notes, and bonds during the review period showed that the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally followed the US dollar against major currencies to be weaker and declined (Figure 4.4). Due to the small difference in inflation rates between Hong Kong and its trading partners and the limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the trend of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index generally follows the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.4 forecasts the nominal and real effective exchange rate outlook, and uncertain factors related to the development of the epidemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the continued tension in China and the United States, may exacerbate fluctuations in capital flows. As an international financial center, various fundraising activities (such as new share offerings) take place in Hong Kong, resulting in a large inflow and outflow of funds to and from Hong Kong. On the one hand, related fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by the listed company may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong due to business needs. Hong Kong possesses sufficient foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, capable of withstanding fluctuations in capital flows without affecting financial stability. Amidst the continuous inflow of Hong Kong dollar, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. In the eight months from the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar's currency basis increased by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). By component analysis, the increase in the currency base during this period reflects the increase in total reserves triggered by multiple activations of the strength-based exchange guarantee. On the other hand, other components, including debt certificates, government-issued circulating banknotes and coins, as well as outstanding foreign exchange fund notes and bonds, remain relatively stable. The components of the currency base in Figure 4.5 increased the Hong Kong dollar deposits derived from new share offerings during the review period, causing the Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit components to rise significantly from July 2020 to October 2021 (Figure 4.6). Following the conclusion of the new share offerings activities and the repayment of new share offerings, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad currency returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, the Hong Kong dollar M3 increased significantly again, mainly driven by the large new share offerings activities during July 2020 to October 2021. Overall, over the seven months from the end of June, the Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the new share offerings activities in July 2020, the Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 9.1%. Based on the corresponding asset analysis, if new share offerings are excluded, the growth of Hong Kong dollar M3 is mainly due to the strength-based exchange guarantee being triggered, which drives an increase in the currency base (Figure 4.7). As a main component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased by 22.9% during the same period, and excluding the impact of new share offerings activities in July 2020, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit interest rates, this was entirely offset by the rapid growth of current and savings deposits driven by investment demand. Figure 4.6 shows approved institution deposits by currency, and Figure 4.7 shows the overall foreign currency deposits of Hong Kong dollar M3 and corresponding asset changes, which have steadily increased by 3.6% over the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits slightly decreased by 0.3%, partially reflecting a weakness in the US dollar, while deposits in other foreign currencies grew strongly by 15.5% during the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in RMB deposits. Overall, due to the short-term fluctuation in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by new share offerings activities, the total deposits of the securities firms increased significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Figure 4.6). Excluding the new share offerings activities in July 2020, total deposits grew by 6.4%. It should be noted that because monthly currency statistics may be affected by various short-term factors (such as seasonality, public offering-related capital demands, and business and investment activities), the statistical figures should be interpreted with caution. As total reserves increased, interbank lending rates at the Hong Kong bank remained at extremely low levels overall during the review period (Figure 4.8). Although there were large new share offerings activities in the second half of 2020, due to ample liquidity in the banking system, interbank lending rates from Hong Kong banks did not experience significant fluctuations. Overall, the banking industry in Hong Kong continues to operate normally. Figure 4.8 The Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank lending rates yield curves generally follow the trend of the US dollar yield curve, becoming steeper during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Figure 4.9). Compared to the end of June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong government bonds slightly decreased by 4 basis points to 0.23% by the end of February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong government bonds rose by 67 basis points during the same period to 1.30%. The Hong Kong dollar interest rates for government bonds, composite rates, and average loan rates for new mortgages in the retail sector mainly fell in Hong Kong dollar in line with the decline in interbank lending rates. Figure 4.9 The composite rates, reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, further declined from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Figure 4.9). Due to the reduction in funding costs, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages decreased from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in July 2021, generally following the trend of the interbank lending rates of the Hong Kong bank during July 2020 to October 2021. On the other hand, the most favorable loan interest rates for retail banks will remain unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the exchange rate system, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the long-term low US interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to remain low and fluctuate due to capital market activity and seasonality liquidity demand. Faced with a highly uncertain macroeconomic financial environment, the ample liquidity of the banking system should be able to provide sufficient buffer to maintain the monetary and financial stability of Hong Kong. The exchange rates of offshore RMB (CNH) and onshore RMB (CNY) against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Figure 4.10), generally reflecting a better economic outlook for inland China compared to other regions in the world, as well as the weakness in the US dollar. FTSE Russell announced at the end of September that mainland Chinese government bonds will be included in the World Government Bond Index, further supporting the strengthening of the RMB investment demand. During most of the review period, the offshore RMB exchange rate had a premium compared to the onshore RMB exchange rate, with an average premium of approximately 100 points in the fourth quarter, which is still considered mild according to historical standards. Figure 4.10, during the review period, the liquidity situation of the offshore RMB industry market for offshore RMB and onshore RMB exchange rate remained stable. Although the overnight offshore RMB interbank lending rates of the Hong Kong bank experienced temporary fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demands and seasonality liquidity demand near the end of the year, they generally remained below 4% (Figure 4.11). The three-month offshore RMB interbank lending rates of the Hong Kong bank followed the onshore RMB interest rates, declining in late December and subsequently rising again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonality. Figure 4.11: In the second half of 2020, the pricing of overnight and three-month offshore RMB interbank lending rates of the Hong Kong bank indicated that Hong Kong's offshore RMB funding pool continued to show an increasing trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth rate of RMB deposits has accelerated, to some extent reflecting the appreciation of the RMB and the relatively higher interest rates of the RMB compared to other monetary currencies. Compared to the end of June 2020, the growth rate of RMB customer deposits and deposit certificate balances accelerated, reaching RMB 826.3 billion at the end of July 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Figure 4.1 and Table 4.A). Of which, RMB customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by the strong growth in company customer deposits. In the relevant transactions, the increase in remittances exported from Hong Kong to Mainland China was higher than the increase in remittances imported from Mainland China to Hong Kong (Figure 4.13). Due to the recurrent COVID-19 pandemic leading to persistent economic downturns, coupled with the impact of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong's retail banks experienced further declines in profitability in the second half of 2020, and asset quality also slightly deteriorated. Nevertheless, based on its capital and liquidity situation, the Hong Kong banking sector remains stable. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy through the difficulties, the Monetary Authority decided to extend several relief measures. Looking ahead, although the introduction of vaccines may inspire optimism that the global pandemic will be controlled and economic activity can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains unclear. The aforementioned uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions will be detrimental to business activities and continue to pose challenges to the Hong Kong banking sector. Especially the pandemic will weaken the repayment capacity of enterprises and households, and the banking industry should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on the quality of its assets. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared to the same period in 2019. Accordingly, the return on assets fell to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared to 1.13% in the same period in 2019 (Figure 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.2), causing a decrease in net interest income and exceeding the slight increase in non-interest income, leading to a decline in profitability. For the full year 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks declined by 29.4%, and the return on assets fell from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Figure 5.1 retail banks profitability Figure 5.2 the net interest margin of retail banks is largely driven by the influx of a large amount of funds due to stock market activity, making Hong Kong dollar liquidity more abundant. The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflects the decrease in funding costs for peer banks and the lowering of fixed deposit interest rates by some major retail banks. Figure 5.3, from a broader perspective, the average overall funding costs in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar for licensed banks in Hong Kong experienced a moderate decrease of 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Figure 5.4). Furthermore, although vaccine research has achieved breakthroughs, increasing optimism in the market regarding the global economic outlook, there remain considerable uncertainties based on the allocation and efficacy of vaccines, and the trajectory of the economic recovery remains extremely unclear. The aforementioned risk factors will continue to affect the credit quality and profitability of the banking industry in the near term. The capital of the Hong Kong banking sector remains sound and far exceeds the minimum international standards of the banking industry. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally registered licensed institutions was 20.7% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the international minimum requirement of 8% (Figure 5.5). The one-year capital adequacy ratio is 18.7%, of which 16.7% is common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. The novel coronavirus pandemic caused a massive impact on the global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-end funds experienced significant capital outflows (Figure B1.1), posing a pressure on their liquidity management. (Figure B1.1) During the events of March 2020, in addition to the liquidity needs of investors, another reason for the large-scale capital outflows from some open-end funds may have been investors redeeming the funds early to take advantage of a "first-mover advantage," thereby avoiding potentially surging redemption costs under market stress. To curb capital outflows induced by the first-mover advantage, some open-end funds adopt swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-end funds that mitigates the first-mover advantage for investors. Although many open-end funds have used swing pricing in the secondary market, there is no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce the outflow of open-end funds. In this context, this study conducts empirical research to understand whether swing pricing can reduce capital outflows from open-end funds in the events of March 2020, thereby lowering their liquidity risk. Furthermore, this study will also seek factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we will propose policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming earlier than other investors, thereby passing the redemption costs onto them. The first-mover advantage primarily exists in open-end funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, where the subscription and redemption costs for the investors of the fund (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-end fund price after the transaction takes place. Under this pricing mechanism, investors redeeming shares shall not be subject to those transaction costs. This became the incentive for them to redeem the fund early, especially in the case of anticipated large redemption costs. Therefore, during market stress, the first-mover advantage will be more pronounced due to the expectation of rising redemption costs. This expands the redemption pressure and liquidity risk faced by open-end funds.

Climate change affects every aspect of life, and each individual has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating the impacts of climate change. In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has invested significant effort in promoting Hong Kong's climate goals and is contributing to enhancing global climate change response capabilities and sustainable development. Following last year when we included the first sustainable development report in the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's 2021 Annual Report as one chapter, this year we will publish the 2022 sustainable development report separately for the first time. I hope this report will allow readers to gain a deeper understanding of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's strategies and key focus areas regarding strengthening the Hong Kong banking system's capacity to address Climate change, build a green financial ecosystem, and how to implement work strategies in areas such as responsible investment and sustainable development organizations. During the year, we have made significant progress in advancing the sustainable development work of the main functions of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. Everyone will learn about our specific measures and work in this report, with the main points being the following: the bank's daily operations face climate risks. As a banking regulatory body, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has taken specific measures to strengthen banks' capacity to address climate change. In 2022, we developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risks into regulatory procedures and to research how to leverage the power of technology to assist banks in assessing the impact of physical risks. Having seen banks launch more and more green and sustainable products, we also shared best practices on how to properly manage these products with the industry to promote the ability of banks to strengthen their climate risks management. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority actively participates in cooperative programs related to addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance development. Locally, we are collaborating with other financial regulatory bodies through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Inter-agency Steering Group" (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework. The framework will increase the transparency of the financial markets and make green financial policies more consistent. At the international level, we are actively participating in several different international organizations to assist in formulating policies to address climate change and assessing its impact on financial stability. Hong Kong possesses the conditions to meet the Asia region's demand for green and sustainable financing. Although 2022 was a challenging year for the global bond market, the issuance amount of green and sustainable debt in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly, with an increase of 42% to a total issuance amount of US$80.5 billion, making it the largest hub in the Asia region for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The relevant issuers include the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the Hainan Provincial People's Government, whose issuance once again demonstrates Hong Kong's unique role in promoting green and sustainable financial flows between the mainland and international markets. The Hong Kong green bond market is thriving, partly attributable to the government's green bond programme. Since 2019, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has assisted the government in issuing green bonds valued at nearly $16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy saving. We also assisted the government in achieving a "first" in two areas, including in May 2022, assisting the government in issuing the first batch of government green retail bonds totaling HK$20 billion, which was the largest green retail bond issuance globally at that time. Additionally, we also assisted the government in issuing the first tranche of tokenized green bonds in February 2023. This is the first batch of tokenized green bonds issued by the government, and the subsequent issuance also marks a milestone in our successful combination of advantages in the bond market, green, sustainable finance, and financial technology. Standards, data, and human resources are indispensable elements driving the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and this requires the efforts and cooperation of various sectors to be established. For this purpose, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority primarily cooperates with the Steering Group and other relevant government departments, regulatory bodies, academic institutions, and the financial industry to expand the aforementioned elements. In addition to the establishment of the local green classification framework mentioned above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training in the industry and improves Hong Kong's data resources through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Centre" established under its umbrella. Furthermore, the Steering Group has also made good progress in other areas such as the mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority further strengthened the work of foreign exchange funds in responsible investment, particularly by setting the target for foreign exchange fund investment portfolios to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we have also optimized risk management to enhance the climate response capability and risk-adjusted long-term returns of the foreign exchange funds. Furthermore, to fully seize the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investments in foreign exchange funds, seeking investment opportunities that support climate transition and mitigate climate change, in order to enhance the long-term returns of the investment portfolio. By the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon density of the foreign exchange funds stock portfolio decreased by 43% compared to the level in 2017. In fact, foreign exchange funds continue to bear lower risk concerning high-carbon assets compared to the overall market. In the future, we will continue to integrate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercise ownership of assets, and continuously collaborate with all stakeholders, focusing on the decarbonization and transformation of the investment portfolio to continue moving towards the net-zero emissions goal. At the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the "Institutional Social Responsibility and Sustainable Development Committee," chaired by me, is responsible for formulating the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's sustainable development strategy. Our strategic direction is based on the three pillars of environmental, employee, and social responsibility. In terms of the environmental aspect, we are committed to promoting a green work environment and promoting more environmentally friendly markets to the social public. In terms of employees, as an employer who bears the responsibility for and cares for employees, we actively create a healthy and inclusive environmental work environment. In terms of social responsibility, we are committed to improving the public's financial knowledge level, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to society. Compared to the levels when we began tracking carbon footprint in 2015, the per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption, and paper usage in 2022 have all achieved double-digit reductions. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions, and using 2015 as a baseline, to reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier to address climate change and promote sustainable development through continuous and ongoing efforts and cooperation from multiple parties. On this important global issue, we understand that it is necessary to take action through our conduct, and to work together with colleagues and international organizations who share the same principles. In the next section, we will outline the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's short-term plans and key priorities in addressing climate change under its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or sooner is a formidable task, and we will exert our utmost effort to achieve this goal. We are confident that through the joint efforts of all colleagues, the financial industry, and the social public, we can successfully address future climate challenges. Chairman Yu Wei-wen

In 2023, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to promote the sustainable development of the Hong Kong financial industry and fulfill its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainability institution. Concurrently, through participation in international and regional organizations, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will also be committed to promoting the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As a banking regulatory body, we are committed to strengthening the banking sector's climate resilience and further improving our green financial ecosystem to support the green transition of banks. Specifically, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing climate risk management regulatory provisions, to incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review procedures, and to revise the joint assessment framework for the banking sector's "green standards." Concurrently, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will support banks in their work to enhance climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example, by exploring different measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, calculate, and monitor their climate risk exposures. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress testing, as part of the regular stress testing led by the regulatory body for the 2023 to 2024 fiscal year. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to address climate risks according to the optimized stress testing framework. This framework encompasses various stress scenarios, including extreme climate and adverse economic conditions. To promote the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will closely follow local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on sales processes as appropriate. We will also conduct on-site specialized assessments to fully understand the green and sustainable investment products offered by the bank. At the same time, to strengthen the construction of the green financial ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements of developing a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will assist the government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the "Government Green Bond Programme" and broadening the scope of the programme to include sustainable development bonds, in order to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub within the region. Simultaneously, attract more green financing activities to take place in Hong Kong through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Support Scheme." The Hong Kong Monetary Authority also assists in promoting the government-funded "Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Programme" to expand the talent pool for green finance in Hong Kong. Furthermore, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to encourage more mainland local governments, institutions, and enterprises to utilize Hong Kong for green financing and explore the feasibility of combining green finance and technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other organizational departments on cross-industry issues such as skills training and data, green classification directories, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Inter-agency Steering Group." Through the green commercial bank alliance, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will jointly launch various specialized programs with international financial institutions in the Asia region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training to banks, and providing practical guidance to assist banks in developing roadmaps to make green finance a core business. Looking to the future, the alliance will work closely with its foundational members, global partners, and knowledge partners to launch a membership program to expand the alliance's influence in the Asian region. The alliance will also strengthen and enhance the professional capabilities of industry personnel, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead the undertaking of project plans in new areas. As a responsible investor, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has set a target for its foreign exchange fund investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, as a commitment to participate in global climate response work and the work of the group on implementing climate-related financial disclosures. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to incorporate environmental, social, and governance factors into its investment management processes, strive towards the goal of net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate response efforts. As a responsible and sustainable organization, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is concerned not only with its employees but also with the public and the surrounding environment. We have developed a sustainability roadmaps and established climate targets for our own operations, as a commitment to our participation in global carbon reduction and climate response efforts. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to prioritize reducing carbon emissions and encourage employees to fully support energy saving and waste reduction. Furthermore, we will provide further guidance to employees to incorporate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To implement digital transformation and enhance operational flexibility, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will explore methods for modernizing internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency while minimizing potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has always been committed to consolidating the Hong Kong financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks face various impacts related to sustainability and climate in their daily operations. To continue to play its important role in the financial system and guide more capital towards green and sustainability projects, Banks must proactively manage climate risk. As a banking regulatory body, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is particularly focused on building the capacity of Banks to address and manage climate risk, and is accelerating the work of Banks to support the transition to a low-carbon economic model. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority also supports Banks in enhancing their capabilities in detecting environmental crimes and participated in the recently published risk assessment for money laundering and terrorist financing in Hong Kong, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife smuggling. In 2022, the Basel Committee issued effective principles for the management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to common questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers the aforementioned risks for Banks. In response to these international developments, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will continue to strive to incorporate climate-related factors into the regulatory framework. After issuing the "Regulatory Policy Manual" Unit GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has also maintained communication with Banks to exchange views on the expectations, progress, and challenges in implementing the relevant regulatory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of Banks' Climate Risk Management, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into banking supervision procedures and communicated this to the banking sector in June. As part of the two-year plan implementation, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority issued the revised Chapter SA-1 of the "Risk-Based Prudential Regime" in the "Regulatory Policy Manual," and enhanced the CAMEL2 rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based prudential procedures. At the same time, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority improved the climate risk stress testing scenarios and assessment framework based on the experience gained from the pilot program since 2021. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress testing into regular stress tests led by regulatory bodies to conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the resilience of the banking sector under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is also strengthening its green assessment framework for Banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues (including Climate Risk Management and transition planning). Meanwhile, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is reviewing the supervisory review procedures for the second pillar capital requirements, which are used to assess and supervise the capital adequacy of Banks, aiming to encourage Banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address the risks related to Climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the increasing popularity of Banks issuing green and sustainability products, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority conducted a special review, primarily examining the Banks' development and ongoing management of these products. During its special review process, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority identified some good practices and issued a notice in December to share with the industry, encouraging Banks to gradually strengthen their Climate Risk Management capabilities. Applied technology can improve data availability and strengthen the ability of Banks to manage climate risk. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority has begun developing a universal platform for Banks to assess the impact of entity risk on real estate. Furthermore, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, in conjunction with other central banks and regulatory bodies, is exploring how to utilize technological solutions to assist in entity risk assessment for projects under the International Settlement Banking Innovation Network. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority also places great importance on promoting sustainability and leading global anti-money laundering work practices. This aspect of the work employs advanced analytics and compliance technology, supplemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. In the past 12 months, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce the burden on Banks and paper volume. To enhance transparency in the financial markets and ensure greater consistency in green finance policies, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is collaborating with other regulatory bodies to establish a local green classification framework. The green classification framework is generally known as the green classification directory, which classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are truly green or sustainable. Therefore, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will maintain contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to thoroughly explore the features and challenges of this framework, and prepare recommendations and conduct consultations on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is well aware that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system; therefore, broader climate factors and scenarios should be incorporated into financial risk analysis and research to strengthen current supervisory work. In the process of continuously monitoring financial stability risks, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will take into account climate change and include analyses of climate-related risks in all financial stability reports. Through active participation in the working group for scenario design and analysis under the "central banks and regulatory bodies green finance network" (NGFS), the Hong Kong Monetary Authority assists in further enriching climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulatory bodies to gain a clearer understanding of the impact of climate change on the macroeconomy and finance. In terms of research work, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority conducted multiple applied research projects in 2022, deeply exploring two issues: the greenwashing behavior in the corporate green bond market, and the role of disclosure in bearing climate risk. The research findings above are helpful in formulating policies and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Locally, this research helps strengthen the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's continuous monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has shared research findings with various stakeholders through various channels, including international central banks research seminars and the Authority's "Semi-annual Report on Currency and Financial Stability." The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's "Liquidity Funding Arrangement Framework" is a collateralized reserve funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is studying the inclusion of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and promoting sustainability finance as the mainstream.
